nodes.title: INTRODUCTION
nodes.heading: INTRODUCTION
nodes.start_phrase: The following is Management’s discussion and analysis of the financial condition and results of operations (“MD&A”) of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”) for the first quarter of 2021 .
nodes.summary:
- Introduces JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s MD&A for the first quarter of 2021, to be read alongside the 2020 Form 10-K and supported by a glossary and LOB metrics.
- Notes inclusion of forward-looking statements subject to significant risks and uncertainties, with cross-references to related disclosures in this Form 10-Q and the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Provides a firm overview: a Delaware-incorporated (1968) U.S.-based global financial services leader with $3.7 trillion in assets and $280.7 billion in stockholders’ equity as of March 31, 2021, serving consumers, small businesses, and major corporate, institutional, and government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Describes organizational structure and key entities: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 38 states and D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; and principal non-U.S. operating subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.).
- Outlines management reporting segments: four major reportable businesses—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment, with references to notes for detailed segment descriptions.
- Highlights investor communications and access: SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) made available free on the firm’s website shortly after filing, with additional information via the Investor Relations site.

nodes.title: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.heading: EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW
nodes.start_phrase: This executive overview of the MD&A highlights selected information and does not contain all of the information that is important to readers of this Form 10-Q.
nodes.summary:
- Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for Q1 2021 Form 10-Q (unaudited), advising readers to consult the full 10-Q and 2020 10-K for complete trends, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Selected Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020 results: total net revenue $32.3B (+14%), noninterest expense $18.7B (+12%), pre-provision profit $13.5B (+18%), provision for credit losses a net benefit of $4.2B vs a prior-year expense, net income $14.3B (+399%), diluted EPS $4.50 (+477%), ROE 23%, ROTCE 29%, book value per share $82.31, tangible book value per share $66.56.
- Strong capital ratios reflecting Fed COVID-19 relief and CECL transition: CET1 13.1%, Tier 1 15.0%, Total capital 17.2% (with note on prior-period presentation revisions).
- Firmwide highlights: $5.2B reduction in the allowance for credit losses (vs $6.8B addition in prior year) and a $550M contribution to the Firm’s Foundation.
- Revenue drivers: Noninterest revenue $19.4B (+40%) on higher CIB Markets revenue, higher Investment Banking fees, and absence of prior-year losses/markdowns; net interest income $12.9B (−11%) due to lower rates partly offset by balance sheet growth.
- Expense drivers: Up 12% from higher volume- and revenue-related costs, continued business investments, and the $550M Foundation contribution.
- Credit quality and reserves: Total allowance for credit losses $25.6B; allowance coverage to retained loans 2.42% (down from 2.95% QoQ, up from 2.32% YoY); nonperforming assets $10.3B (up $3.2B YoY due to COVID-19 impacts; down $649M QoQ due to portfolio activity, upgrades in Oil & Gas and Individuals, and sales of certain CIB consumer nonaccrual loans at fair value).
- Balance sheet and liquidity: Average loans ~$1.0T (+1%) with growth in AWM and CIB, declines in CCB and CB, and inclusion of PPP loans; average deposits ~$2.2T (+36%) driven by government actions; robust liquidity with ~$697B average HQLA and ~$841B unencumbered marketable securities, totaling about $1.5T in liquidity sources.
- References to detailed sections: Capital Risk Management and Liquidity Risk Management for additional information.

nodes.title: Firmwide overview
nodes.heading: Firmwide overview
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase reported net income of $14.3 billion for the first quarter of 2021 , or $4.50 per share, on net revenue of $32.3 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Executive overview of JPMorgan Chase’s MD&A for Q1 2021, highlighting selected information and advising readers to consult the full Form 10‑Q and 2020 Form 10‑K for complete context, risks, and critical accounting estimates.
- Firmwide financial results (Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020):
  - Net income $14.3B, up $11.4B; diluted EPS $4.50, up 477%.
  - Total net revenue $32.3B, up 14%; noninterest revenue up 40% on stronger CIB Markets, higher Investment Banking fees, and absence of prior‑year losses; net interest income down 11% due to lower rates partially offset by balance sheet growth.
  - Noninterest expense $18.7B, up 12%, reflecting higher volume/revenue‑related costs, continued investments, and a $550M contribution to the Firm’s Foundation.
  - Provision for credit losses a net benefit of $4.2B driven by $5.2B allowance reduction, versus an $8.3B expense in prior year tied to a $6.8B allowance build.
  - Pre‑provision profit $13.5B, up 18%.
  - Returns: ROE 23% and ROTCE 29% (up from 4% and 5%).
  - Book value per share $82.31 (up 8%); tangible book value per share $66.56 (up 10%).
- Credit quality and reserves:
  - Total allowance for credit losses $25.6B; allowance for loan losses to retained loans coverage ratio 2.42% (down from 2.95% in Q4 2020; up from 2.32% YoY).
  - Nonperforming assets $10.3B, up $3.2B YoY due to deterioration across multiple wholesale industries and COVID‑19 impacts on consumer loans; down $649M from Dec 31, 2020, on portfolio activity and upgrades (notably Oil & Gas and Individuals) and sales of certain CIB consumer nonaccrual loans at fair value.
- Balance sheet trends:
  - Average loans ~$1.0T, up 1%, with growth in AWM and CIB, partially offset by declines in CCB and CB; PPP originations contributed in CCB and CB.
  - Average deposits ~$2.2T, up 36%, reflecting significant inflows across LOBs primarily from government actions in response to COVID‑19.
- Liquidity and capital:
  - Average eligible HQLA ~$697B; unencumbered marketable securities ~$841B; total liquidity sources ~ $1.5T.
  - Capital ratios (reflecting Federal Reserve COVID‑19 relief and CECL transition): CET1 13.1%, Tier 1 15.0%, Total capital 17.2%.
- Notes:
  - Certain prior‑period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Comparisons are Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020 unless otherwise specified.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.heading: CONSOLIDATED RESULTS OF OPERATIONS
nodes.start_phrase: This section provides a comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s Consolidated Results of Operations on a reported basis for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020 , unless otherwise specified.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020, with cross-references to segment results, notes, and critical accounting estimates.
- Overall results: Total net revenue up 14% to $32.3B; noninterest revenue up 40% to $19.4B; net interest income down 11% to $12.9B.
- Investment banking fees: Up 59% across products, driven by strong IPO activity (higher industry-wide fees), more completed advisory transactions (including deals announced in late 2020), and higher debt underwriting (high-yield bonds and leveraged loans; wallet share gains).
- Principal transactions: Up 121%, largely due to absence of prior-year losses ($951M in Credit Adjustments & Other and $896M bridge financing markdowns) and strong CIB Markets performance (Equity derivatives, cash equities, prime brokerage; Fixed Income in Securitized Products and Credit; offset by lower Rates and Currencies/EM). Also includes net gains on legacy private equity in Corporate. Notes potential offsets with net interest income; CIB Markets assessed on total revenue basis.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 1%; lower CCB deposit-related fees due to higher balances, partially offset by higher cash management fees in CIB/CB and higher lending-related (loan commitment) fees in CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Up 11%; higher asset management fees from strong net inflows and higher average market levels in AWM (partly offset by liquidity fee waivers) and higher investment assets in CCB.
- Investment securities gains: Down 94%, reflecting investment securities portfolio repositioning.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Up 120% on higher production margins and volumes.
- Card income: Up 36% on lower acquisition costs and higher net interchange as debit and credit card sales returned to pre-pandemic levels.
- Other income: Down 10%; includes operating lease income of $1.3B (vs. $1.4B prior year). Prior-period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
- References: Points readers to CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, and Corporate segment sections and Notes 1, 5, 9, and 14 for further details; cites critical accounting estimates sections in the 10-Q and 2020 10-K.

nodes.title: Revenue
nodes.heading: Revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Investment banking fees increased across products in CIB, reflecting:
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Comparative discussion of JPMorgan Chase’s consolidated results for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020, with cross-references to segment details and critical accounting estimates.
- Total net revenue: Up 14% to $32.3B, driven by a 40% increase in noninterest revenue; net interest income declined 11%.
- Investment banking fees: Up 59% to $3.0B, reflecting stronger equity underwriting (IPOs), increased advisory from more completed deals, and higher debt underwriting (high-yield and leveraged loans) amid higher industry fees and wallet share gains (CIB).
- Principal transactions revenue: Up 121% to $6.5B, aided by absence of two large prior-year losses (CIB Credit Adjustments & Other and bridge financing markdowns). Excluding these, growth came from strong Equity Markets (derivatives, cash equities, prime brokerage) and Fixed Income Markets (securitized products, credit), partly offset by lower Rates and Currencies & EM; also net gains on legacy private equity in Corporate. Note that CIB Markets performance is assessed on total revenue, given offsets with net interest income.
- Lending- and deposit-related fees: Down 1%, as lower deposit-related fees in CCB (from higher balances) were largely offset by higher cash management fees in CIB/CB and higher lending-related/commitment fees in CIB.
- Asset management, administration and commissions: Up 11% to $5.0B, driven by higher AWM fees from strong net inflows into long-term and liquidity products and higher market levels (net of liquidity fee waivers), plus higher investment assets in CCB.
- Investment securities gains: Down 94% to $14MM, reflecting portfolio repositioning.
- Mortgage fees and related income: Up 120% to $704MM on higher production margins and volumes (CCB).
- Card income: Up 36% to $1.35B on lower acquisition costs and higher net interchange as debit/credit spend returned to pre-pandemic levels (CCB).
- Other income: Down 10% to $1.12B, due to weather-related write-downs and higher amortization in tax-oriented renewable energy investments (offset in part by related tax credits), lower gains on certain Corporate investments, and lower auto operating lease income in CCB; partially offset by valuation gains in AWM and the absence of prior-year losses on certain CIB equity investments. Footnote notes operating lease income of $1.3B (2021) vs. $1.4B (2020).
- Net interest income: Down 11% to $12.9B, predominantly from lower rates, partly offset by balance sheet growth. Average interest-earning assets rose $661B to $3.1T; yield fell 127 bps to 1.87%. Net yield (FTE) fell 68 bps to 1.69%; excluding CIB Markets, net yield fell 108 bps to 1.93% (non-GAAP measures referenced).
- Provision for credit losses: Swing to a net release of $4.16B vs. an $8.29B build in prior year, driven by reductions in both consumer and wholesale allowances.
  - Consumer: $3.50B net release vs. $5.68B build, reflecting a $4.5B allowance reduction (including $3.5B in Card from improved macroeconomic scenarios and $625MM in Home Lending from improved HPI and portfolio runoff), lower Card net charge-offs helped by payment assistance and government stimulus, and comparison to a $4.4B prior-year build.
  - Wholesale: $671MM net release vs. $2.59B build, reflecting a $716MM allowance reduction on improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- Repeated references to segment-level discussions (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate) and notes for further detail, including non-GAAP reconciliations and credit allowance disclosures.

nodes.title: Provision for credit losses
nodes.heading: Provision for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The provision for credit losses decreased driven by net reductions in both the consumer and wholesale allowance for credit losses.
nodes.summary:
- Other income decreased, driven by weather-related write-downs and higher amortization on alternative energy investments in CIB (with tax credits reducing tax expense), lower gains on certain Corporate investments, and lower operating lease income in CCB; partially offset by valuation gains in AWM and the absence of prior-year equity investment losses in CIB.
- Net interest income declined primarily due to lower rates, partly offset by balance sheet growth. Average interest-earning assets rose to $3.1 trillion (+$661 billion), with yield down to 1.87% (-127 bps). Net yield on an FTE basis was 1.69% (-68 bps); excluding CIB Markets, 1.93% (-108 bps). These yields are non-GAAP measures with further details referenced.
- Provision for credit losses swung to a net release of $4.2 billion in Q1 2021 versus an $8.3 billion build in Q1 2020. By category: consumer excluding credit card $(984) million, credit card $(2,517) million, total consumer $(3,501) million, wholesale $(671) million, and investment securities $16 million.
- The consumer reserve release reflected a $4.5 billion reduction in allowances (including $3.5 billion in Card on improved macroeconomic scenarios and $625 million in Home Lending on better HPI expectations and portfolio runoff), lower net charge-offs in Card aided by payment assistance and government stimulus, and the absence of a prior-year $4.4 billion addition.
- Wholesale reserves decreased by $716 million across lines of business, reflecting improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- References are provided to segment results, allowance for credit losses, and non-GAAP reconciliations for further detail.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEETS AND CASH FLOWS ANALYSIS

nodes.summary:
- Scope and period: Analysis of significant changes in the consolidated balance sheet between March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020.
- Overall size: Total assets rose 9% to $3.69 trillion.
- Liquidity and cash placement:
  - Cash and due from banks up 2%; deposits with banks up 36% as excess cash was placed with central banks (e.g., Federal Reserve).
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements down 8% due to lower Treasury/CIO deployment and lower client market-making, partly offset by higher demand to cover short positions.
- Securities financing and trading:
  - Securities borrowed up 12% on client-driven activity and short-coverage needs.
  - Trading assets up 8% on strong client-driven equity market-making, including prime brokerage.
- Investment portfolio:
  - Investment securities up 1%; HTM securities (notably U.S. Treasuries) increased, while AFS securities fell 2% due to paydowns and net valuation losses partially offset by purchases.
- Loans:
  - Gross loans flat overall.
  - Declines in Card (seasonality, higher payment rates), Commercial Banking, and home lending paydowns were offset by PPP originations (CBB and CB), growth in CIB loans held-for-sale/at fair value, AWM securities-based and custom lending, and mortgages.
  - Loans, net of allowance, remained essentially unchanged.
- Credit loss reserves:
  - Allowance for loan losses decreased 19% (from $28.3B to $23.0B).
  - Drivers: $4.5B reduction in consumer (primarily credit cards; residential real estate improved on higher HPI and portfolio runoff) and $875M net reduction in wholesale across LOBs as macroeconomic scenarios improved.
  - $107M addition to the allowance for lending-related commitments (in other liabilities).
  - Total net reduction in allowance for credit losses: $5.2B as of March 31, 2021.
- Other notable line items:
  - Accrued interest and accounts receivable up 27%.
  - Other assets up 32% (prior period revised to conform to current presentation).
  - Goodwill/MSRs/other intangibles up 2%; premises and equipment down 1%.
- References: Mentions Liquidity Risk Management and various Notes/segment discussions for further detail.

nodes.title: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.heading: Consolidated balance sheets analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The following is a discussion of the significant changes between M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Analysis of significant changes in the consolidated balance sheet between March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, highlighting key asset, liability, and equity movements and their business drivers.
- Scale: Total assets up 9% to $3.69T; total liabilities up 10% to $3.41T; stockholders’ equity flat at ~$281B.
- Assets:
  - Cash and due from banks and deposits with banks up (cash/deposits with central banks) due to strong deposit growth and fewer opportunities to deploy in reverse repos.
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements down on lower Treasury/CIO deployment and reduced CIB market-making, partly offset by higher demand to cover short positions.
  - Securities borrowed up on client-driven financing and short-cover demand in CIB prime brokerage/markets.
  - Trading assets up on strong client-driven equity market-making, including prime brokerage.
  - Investment securities slightly higher: net HTM U.S. Treasury purchases offset by AFS declines from paydowns and valuation losses (partly offset by net purchases).
  - Loans flat: seasonal/card paydowns, lower CB loans, and Home Lending paydowns offset by PPP originations (CBB/CB), CIB loans held-for-sale/at fair value, and AWM securities-based/custom lending and mortgages.
  - Allowance for loan losses down 19% ($28.3B to $23.0B): $4.5B reduction in consumer (card; residential real estate aided by improved HPI and runoff) and $875MM net reduction in wholesale on improved macro scenarios; $107MM added to allowance for lending-related commitments; net ACL reduction of $5.2B.
  - Accrued interest and receivables up on higher CIB prime brokerage client receivables.
  - Goodwill/MSRs/other intangibles up on higher MSRs (slower prepayments with higher rates) and net additions.
  - Other assets up on securities financing in CIB prime brokerage and higher CCP cash collateral.
- Liabilities:
  - Deposits up 6% across LOBs, driven by government actions tied to COVID-19, lower spending, and account growth (consumer/small business).
  - Federal funds purchased and repos up 41% from higher secured financing of AFS in Treasury/CIO, higher CIB trading assets, and client activity.
  - Short-term borrowings up 22% from prime brokerage financing, net issuance of CIB structured notes, and Treasury/CIO commercial paper issuance.
  - Trading liabilities up 12% on client-driven Fixed Income market-making (higher short positions), partly offset by lower derivative payables.
  - Accounts payable and other liabilities up 23% due to CIB prime brokerage securities financing.
  - Beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs down 11% on lower issuances tied to reduced multi-seller conduit loan balances.
  - Long-term debt roughly flat (maturities and higher-rate hedge adjustments offset by net issuance).
- Equity and AOCI:
  - Stockholders’ equity flat as net income was offset by capital actions and lower AOCI; AOCI decline driven by higher rates impacting AFS securities and cash flow hedges.
- Themes and references:
  - Liquidity deployment shifted toward central bank deposits; elevated client-driven prime brokerage and market-making activity influenced multiple line items.
  - Improved macroeconomic outlook drove sizeable reserve releases.
  - Multiple cross-references to Liquidity, Credit and Investment Risk Management, and relevant financial statement notes.

  - 2020: Cash used for net purchases of investment securities, net loan originations, and purchases of assets from money market mutual fund clients under the FRBB’s MMLF.
- Financing activities drivers:

nodes.title: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.heading: BUSINESS SEGMENT RESULTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm is managed on an LOB basis.
nodes.summary:
- JPMorgan Chase reports performance by lines of business (LOBs): Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates financial information.
- Results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis, with references to the firm’s non-GAAP reconciliation for definitions.
- Segment reporting treats each LOB as a stand-alone business, allocating certain income and expenses to reflect economic performance.
- Assumptions, methodologies, and reporting classifications are periodically reassessed and may be refined in future periods.
- The firm assesses capital needs for each LOB at least annually and provides business metrics used by management, investors, and analysts to evaluate performance.
- Revenue sharing is applied when multiple segments collaborate: revenue is recognized in the segment responsible for the product/service, with allocations to participating segments.
- Capital (equity) is assigned to each segment; allocation methodologies are reviewed periodically and can change, with further detail referenced in the firm’s 2020 Form 10-K.

nodes.title: Description of business segment reporting methodology
nodes.heading: Description of business segment reporting methodology
nodes.start_phrase: Results of the business segments are intended to present each segment as if it were a stand-alone business.
nodes.summary:
- The firm reports and manages performance by line of business, with four major reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, and Asset & Wealth Management—plus a Corporate segment.
- Segments are defined by products/services or customer type and align with how the Operating Committee evaluates financial information.
- Results are presented on a managed (non-GAAP) basis; references are provided for the definition and reconciliations.
- Segment reporting methodology presents each LOB as a stand‑alone business, allocating certain income and expense items; assumptions, methodologies, and classifications are reviewed and refined periodically.
- The firm assesses capital needs for each LOB at least annually and provides business metrics used by management, investors, and analysts to evaluate performance.
- Revenue sharing: when multiple segments collaborate on client transactions, revenue is recognized by the segment owning the product/service with allocations to participating segments; segment results reflect these agreements.
- Capital allocation: equity is assigned to each segment; allocation methodologies are periodically reassessed and may change LOB capital levels; additional details and references to the 2020 Form 10‑K are provided.

- Performance highlights:
  - Net income: $6.7B, up $6.5B year-over-year, driven by a net benefit in credit provisions.
  - Total net revenue: $12.5B, down 6%.
  - Return on equity: 54% (vs 1%).
  - Overhead ratio: 58 (vs 55).

- Revenue drivers:
  - Net interest income: $7.9B, down 14%, reflecting deposit margin compression in Consumer & Business Banking (CBB), lower Card loans (reduced spend and higher payment rates), and lower Home Lending balances due to paydowns; partially offset by strong deposit growth in CBB.
  - Noninterest revenue: $4.6B, up 12%, led by:
    - Higher mortgage production revenue on stronger margins and volumes.
    - Higher card income from lower acquisition costs and higher net interchange; debit/credit sales returned to pre-pandemic levels.
    - Offsets: lower deposit-related fees amid higher balances; lower auto lease volume.
  - Specific line items: lending/deposit fees down 24%; mortgage fees and related income up 120% (production revenue up 137%; net MSR revenue negative, with MSR risk management losses of $115M vs $90M); card income up 53%; asset management/administration/commissions up 14%; all other income down 7%.

- Expenses:
  - Noninterest expense: $7.2B, flat (-1%), with higher business investments offset by lower structural costs and lower volume/revenue-related expenses, including reduced auto lease depreciation.
  - Depreciation on leased assets: $916M (vs $1.1B).

- Credit provisions:
  - Provision for credit losses: net benefit of $3.6B (vs $5.8B expense), driven by a $4.6B reduction in allowance for credit losses:
    - Card: $3.5B release.
    - Home Lending: $625M release (improved HPI expectations; portfolio runoff).
    - CBB: $350M release.
    - Auto: $150M release.
  - Lower net charge-offs in Card, aided by payment assistance and government stimulus.

- Revenue by line of business:

  - Home Lending: $1.46B, up 26%.
  - Card & Auto: $5.42B, down 7%.

- Balance sheet and volume metrics (period-end unless noted):

    - Home Lending: $178.8B, down 13% (average down 14%).

  - Deposits: $1.04T, up 32% (average: $980B, up 32%).

  - Home Lending HFS/fair value: $13.2B (average $12.5B).

- Credit quality:

  - Net charge-offs: $1.02B, down 22%; total NCO rate 0.99% (vs 1.18%).
    - CBB: $65M; NCO rate 0.53% (includes PPP loans; SBA guarantee limits losses).
    - Home Lending: net recoveries of $51M; NCO rate -0.12%.
    - Card: $983M; NCO rate 2.97% (vs 3.25%).
    - Auto: $26M; NCO rate 0.16% (vs 0.32%).
  - Delinquencies improved:

    - Card 30+ DPD: 1.40% (vs 1.96%); 90+ DPD: 0.80% (vs 1.02%).
    - Auto 30+ DPD: 0.42% (vs 0.89%).
  - Allowance for loan losses: $17.45B, down 7%:

    - Home Lending: $1.24B (-42%).
    - CBB: $1.02B (+16%).
    - Auto: $0.89B (+22%).
  - COVID-19 payment deferrals at 3/31/21: Home Lending $8.1B; Card $105M; Auto $127M; loans performing to modified terms generally not delinquent.

- References and notes:

nodes.start_phrase: Capital risk is the risk the Firm has an insufficient level or composition of capital to support the Firm’s business activities and associated risks during normal economic environments and under stressed conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk and notes JPMorgan Chase remained well-capitalized through COVID-19; references to 2020 Form 10-K, this Form 10-Q, and Pillar 3 disclosures for more detail.
- Basel III overview: explains risk-weighted assets and the two RWA approaches (Standardized and Advanced); the Firm’s capital adequacy is tested against the lower of the two; currently the Standardized approach is the binding constraint. Mentions SLR requirement for Advanced Approach firms.
- CECL regulatory capital transition: Firm elected the two-year delay with three-year phase-in; for 1Q21 capital metrics exclude $4.5B (comprising $2.7B day-1 retained earnings impact and 25% of the $7.0B ACL increase since Jan 1, 2020, excluding PCD loans). Effects flow through Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
- Temporary SLR relief: BHCs temporarily excluded on-balance sheet U.S. Treasuries and Fed deposits from total leverage exposure from Apr 1, 2020 to Mar 31, 2021. IDIs had an option to apply; JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect it.
- PPP treatment: zero percent risk weight for PPP loans; Firm held about $32B of PPP loans as of Mar 31, 2021 and expects immaterial credit losses; loans included in SLR exposure since the Firm did not use the PPPL Facility.
- TLAC holdings rule: expands capital deduction framework to include TLAC debt of systemically important banks; effective Apr 1, 2021; not expected to materially affect the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.

nodes.title: Basel III Overview
nodes.heading: Basel III Overview
nodes.start_phrase: The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for large and internationally active U.S. Bank Holding Companies ("BHCs") and banks, including the Firm and its insured depository institution (“IDI”) subsidiaries, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as the possibility that the Firm’s capital level or composition is insufficient to support its activities and risks in normal and stressed conditions; notes COVID-19 impacts but that the Firm remains well-capitalized.
- Points to additional disclosures in the 2020 Form 10-K, this Form 10-Q, and Pillar 3 reports for capital planning and stress testing details.
- Outlines Basel III framework: capital requirements based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two methods—Standardized and Advanced—and capital adequacy assessed against the more binding of the two.
- States the Firm’s Basel III Standardized risk-based ratios are currently more binding than the Advanced approach.
- Notes Advanced Approach institutions must calculate the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
- Describes CECL regulatory capital transition: optional two-year delay beginning Jan 1, 2020 with a three-year phase-in from Jan 1, 2022; the Firm elected this, excluding $4.5B from capital metrics as of Mar 31, 2021 ($2.7B day-one retained earnings impact plus 25% of a $7.0B allowance increase). These effects flow through Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
- Details temporary SLR relief: from Apr 1, 2020 to Mar 31, 2021, BHCs could exclude on-balance sheet U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve Bank deposits from total leverage exposure; IDI subsidiaries had an optional exclusion under a parallel rule. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect the IDI exclusion.
- Explains PPP capital treatment: zero percent risk weight applied to PPP loans, limiting impact on risk-based ratios; Firm held about $32B of PPP loans as of Mar 31, 2021 and does not expect material credit losses due to SBA guarantees. PPP loans remain in SLR exposure because the Firm did not use the PPPL Facility.
- Summarizes TLAC holdings rule effective Apr 1, 2021: expands capital deduction treatment to holdings of TLAC debt of systemically important banks; not expected to materially affect the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.

nodes.title: Key Regulatory Developments
nodes.heading: Key Regulatory Developments
nodes.start_phrase: As part of their response to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal banking agencies issued a final rule that provided the option beginning January 1, 2020 to delay the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, followed by a three-year transition period beginning January 1, 2022 (“CECL capital transition provisions”).
nodes.summary:
- Defines capital risk as insufficient capital level/composition to support business and risks in normal and stressed environments; notes COVID-19 impacts but that the Firm remained well-capitalized; references 2020 Form 10-K, this 10-Q Note 21, and Pillar 3 reports for more detail.
- Basel III overview:
  - Regulatory capital based on risk-weighted assets (RWA) using two methods: Basel III Standardized and Basel III Advanced.
  - The Firm’s capital adequacy is assessed against the lower (more binding) of the two; currently the Standardized approach is more binding.
  - Advanced Approach firms, including the Firm, must also calculate the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
- Key regulatory developments:
  - CECL regulatory capital transition: optional two-year delay plus three-year phase-in; the Firm elected the transition, excluding $4.5 billion from capital metrics as of March 31, 2021 (comprising the $2.7 billion day 1 retained earnings impact and 25% of the $7.0 billion increase in the allowance for credit losses, excluding PCD loans). Effects incorporated into Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure.
  - Temporary SLR revision: from April 1, 2020 to March 31, 2021, BHCs could exclude on-balance-sheet U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve deposits from total leverage exposure; the Firm applied this at the holding company level. An IDI-level option was also provided for the same period, which JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. did not elect.
  - Paycheck Protection Program (PPP): zero percent risk weight applied to PPP loans for risk-based capital; Firm held about $32 billion of PPP loans as of March 31, 2021 and does not expect material credit losses due to SBA guarantees. PPP loans are included in total leverage exposure since the Firm did not use the Federal Reserve’s PPPL Facility.
  - TLAC Holdings rule: effective April 1, 2021; extends capital deduction treatment to holdings of TLAC debt of systemically important banks; not expected to materially impact the Firm’s risk-based capital metrics.
- Capital metrics (March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020), reflecting CECL transition and PPP zero risk weight:
  - CET1 capital: $206.1B (vs. $205.1B).
  - RWA: $1.577T Standardized (vs. $1.561T); $1.504T Advanced (vs. $1.484T).
  - Ratios (Standardized; Advanced): CET1 13.1%; 13.7–13.8; Tier 1 15.0%; 15.8; Total capital 17.2–17.3; 17.2–17.3. Minimum requirements including buffers shown for comparison (e.g., CET1 mins approx. 11.3% Standardized; 10.5% Advanced).
  - Leverage-based: Tier 1 leverage ratio 6.7% (vs. 7.0%; minimum 4.0%). SLR 6.7% (vs. 6.9%; minimum 5.0%) with temporary relief; without relief, SLR would be 5.5% (vs. 5.8%).
- Emphasizes that Standardized risk-based ratios are the binding constraint and that temporary COVID-related regulatory adjustments (CECL transition and SLR relief) and PPP capital treatment affected reported capital and leverage measures.

nodes.title: Capital components
nodes.heading: Capital components
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents reconciliations of total stockholders’ equity to Basel III CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital and Total capital as of M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2020 .
nodes.summary:
- Presents Basel III capital components and reconciliations from total stockholders’ equity to CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, under both the Standardized and Advanced approaches.
- Details the reconciliation steps: deduct preferred stock; add certain deferred tax liabilities; include other CET1 adjustments; deduct goodwill and other intangibles; then derive Standardized/Advanced CET1, add preferred stock and subtract other Tier 1 adjustments to get Tier 1 capital.
- Breaks out Tier 2 capital components: qualifying long-term debt and other instruments, qualifying allowance for credit losses (ACL), and other items, yielding Standardized and Advanced Tier 2 and Total capital figures.
- Key results:
  - CET1 capital: $206.1B at 3/31/21 vs. $205.1B at 12/31/20.
  - Tier 1 capital: $237.3B vs. $234.8B.
  - Standardized Tier 2: $34.1B vs. $35.1B; Standardized Total capital: $271.4B vs. $269.9B.
  - Advanced Tier 2: $21.3B vs. $22.4B; Advanced Total capital: $258.6B vs. $257.2B.
- Footnote explanations:
  - Certain deferred tax liabilities tied to tax-deductible goodwill and identifiable intangibles are netted against those assets when calculating CET1.
  - CECL capital transition provision increased CET1 by $4.5B at 3/31/21 and $5.7B at 12/31/20.
  - Tier 2 ACL eligibility capped at 1.25% of credit risk RWA (Standardized), with excess deducted from RWA.
  - Advanced approach includes an adjustment for excess eligible credit reserves over expected credit losses up to 0.6% of credit risk RWA, with any excess deducted from RWA; both include CECL transition impacts.
- Provides a Q1 2021 capital rollforward:
  - CET1 bridge from $205.1B to $206.1B driven by: net income $13.9B; dividends $(2.8)B; net treasury stock purchases $(4.0)B; APIC change $(0.4)B; AOCI change $(6.9)B; AOCI adjustment +$2.4B (cash flow hedges and DVA on structured notes); other CET1 adjustments $(1.3)B; CECL transition effects included.
  - Tier 1 increases by $2.5B to $237.3B, reflecting the $1.0B CET1 increase plus $1.5B net issuance of noncumulative perpetual preferred stock.
  - Tier 2 declines: Standardized down $1.0B to $34.1B (lower qualifying long-term debt, modest ACL increase); Advanced down $1.1B to $21.3B.
  - Resulting Total capital at 3/31/21: $271.4B (Standardized) and $258.6B (Advanced).

nodes.title: Capital rollforward
nodes.heading: Capital rollforward
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the changes in Basel III CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital and Tier 2 capital for the three months ended M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Reconciliation of GAAP stockholders’ equity to Basel III regulatory capital (CET1, Tier 1, and Tier 2), under both Standardized and Advanced approaches, plus a Q1 2021 capital rollforward.
- Periods covered: Balances as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020; changes for the three months ended March 31, 2021.
- CET1 reconciliation: Starts from total stockholders’ equity, subtracts preferred stock to get common equity, adds certain deferred tax liabilities and other CET1 adjustments, and deducts goodwill and other intangibles to arrive at CET1.
  - Key balances at March 31, 2021: CET1 capital $206.1B; Tier 1 capital $237.3B; Standardized Tier 2 capital $34.1B; Standardized Total capital $271.4B; Advanced Tier 2 capital $21.3B; Advanced Total capital $258.6B.
- Key comparative movements vs Dec 31, 2020:
  - Tier 1 capital increased (to $237.3B) driven by higher CET1 and $1.5B preferred issuance.
  - Tier 2 capital decreased under both approaches, mainly from lower qualifying long-term debt.
- Q1 2021 CET1 rollforward drivers:
  - Net income to common +$13.9B.
  - Dividends on common −$2.8B.
  - Net share repurchases −$4.0B.
  - APIC changes −$0.4B.
  - AOCI change −$6.9B, partially offset by AOCI adjustment (cash flow hedges and DVA) +$2.4B.
  - Other CET1 adjustments −$1.3B.
  - Net CET1 increase +$1.0B to $206.1B.
- Q1 2021 Tier 1 and Tier 2 rollforwards:
  - Tier 1: +$2.5B (CET1 +$1.0B; preferred issuance +$1.5B; minor other −$0.0B).
  - Standardized Tier 2: −$1.0B (−$1.0B qualifying long-term debt; +$0.1B allowance; other −$0.1B).
  - Advanced Tier 2: −$1.1B (similar drivers; smaller allowance change).
- CECL capital transition effects:
  - Increased CET1 by $4.5B at March 31, 2021 ($5.7B at Dec 31, 2020).
  - Affects Tier 2 through eligibility limits on allowance for credit losses.
- Allowance for credit losses in capital:
  - Standardized: included in Tier 2 up to 1.25% of credit risk RWA (excess deducted from RWA).
  - Advanced: adjustment for excess eligible credit reserves over expected losses up to 0.6% of credit risk RWA.
- Other technical notes:
  - Deferred tax liabilities related to tax-deductible goodwill and certain intangibles are added back in CET1 (netted against deductions).
  - Goodwill ($49.2B) and other intangibles are deducted from CET1.
  - AOCI note references cash flow hedges and DVA on structured notes.

nodes.title: RWA rollforward
nodes.heading: RWA rollforward
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents changes in the components of RWA under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches for the three months ended M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase’s Q1 2021 regulatory capital metrics, risk-weighted assets (RWA) rollforward, supplementary leverage ratio (SLR), line-of-business capital allocation, and capital actions.
- RWA rollforward (three months ended March 31, 2021):
  - Basel III Standardized: Total RWA increased to $1,577.0B from $1,560.6B (+$16.4B), driven by movement in portfolio levels (+$18.7B) partially offset by model & data changes (-$1.1B, market risk) and credit portfolio runoff (-$1.2B).
  - Basel III Advanced: Total RWA increased to $1,503.8B from $1,484.4B (+$19.4B), primarily from movement in portfolio levels (+$21.2B) offset by model & data changes (-$1.1B, market risk) and portfolio runoff (-$0.7B).
  - Footnotes clarify: model/data changes reflect methodology/treatment updates (not rule changes); portfolio runoff mainly from legacy Home Lending; movement in portfolio levels includes changes in book size/composition/credit quality/market moves, operational risk loss updates, and deductions for excess eligible credit reserves.
- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR):
  - March 31, 2021 vs. Dec 31, 2020: Tier 1 capital $237.3B vs. $234.8B; total leverage exposure $3.523T vs. $3.402T.
  - Reported SLR 6.7% vs. 6.9%; excluding temporary relief (Treasuries and Fed deposits exclusion), SLR 5.5% vs. 5.8%.
  - Components shown include total/adjusted average assets, off-balance sheet exposures (three month-end average), and exclusions for U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve Bank deposits.
- Line of business equity (allocated capital):
  - As of March 31, 2021: CCB $50.0B; CIB $83.0B; Commercial Banking $24.0B; Asset & Wealth Management $14.0B; Corporate $78.2B; total common stockholders’ equity $249.2B.
  - Allocation considers peer capital levels and regulatory requirements.
- Capital actions:
  - Common dividend: $0.90 per share, subject to quarterly Board approval.
  - Share repurchases: Suspended March 2020; Fed halted net repurchases through 2020. Following Dec 18, 2020 Fed guidance, repurchases resumed in Q1 2021 under a new $30B authorization, but combined net repurchases and dividends capped at the average of the prior four quarters’ net income. Fed extended these limits through at least Q2 2021.

nodes.title: Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.heading: Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Supplementary Leverage Ratio on page 95 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for additional information.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt details JPMorgan Chase’s risk-weighted assets (RWA), leverage, capital allocation, and capital actions for the quarter ended March 31, 2021.

- RWA rollforward: Under Basel III Standardized, total RWA rose from $1,560.6B to $1,577.0B (+$16.4B), driven mainly by increases in portfolio levels (+$18.7B; credit +$13.9B, market +$4.8B), partially offset by model/data changes in market risk (−$1.1B) and credit portfolio runoff (−$1.2B). Under Basel III Advanced, total RWA rose from $1,484.4B to $1,503.8B (+$19.4B), with increases across credit (+$11.4B), market (+$4.6B), and operational risk (+$5.1B), offset by market risk model/data changes (−$1.1B) and modest credit portfolio runoff (−$0.7B). Footnotes indicate model/data changes reflect methodology updates per regulatory guidance; portfolio runoff primarily reflects roll-offs in Home Lending; and portfolio level movements (inclusive of rule changes) reflect changes in book size/composition/credit quality/market movements, market risk positions and market moves, operational risk cumulative losses, and certain deductions for excess eligible credit reserves.

- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): Tier 1 capital was $237.3B. Total leverage exposure was $3,522.6B after adjustments, including off-balance-sheet exposures and exclusions for U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve Bank deposits. The SLR was 6.7% (down from 6.9% at 12/31/20). Excluding temporary relief, SLRs were 5.5% and 5.8% for March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, respectively.

- Line of business equity (allocated capital): CCB $50.0B, CIB $83.0B, Commercial Banking $24.0B, Asset & Wealth Management $14.0B, Corporate $78.2B; total common stockholders’ equity $249.2B. Allocation considers peer capital levels and regulatory requirements.

- Capital actions: The quarterly common dividend is $0.90 per share, subject to Board approval. Share repurchases, suspended in March 2020 due to COVID-19 and later restricted by the Federal Reserve, resumed in Q1 2021 under a new $30B authorization, with combined dividends and net repurchases capped by the average of the prior four quarters’ net income; these restrictions were extended at least through Q2 2021.

nodes.heading: Line of business equity

- Line of business equity (allocated capital) as of March 31, 2021 versus December 31, 2020:

- Capital actions:
  - Quarterly common stock dividend of $0.90 per share, subject to Board approval.
  - Share repurchase history and regulatory context: suspension in March 2020 due to COVID-19; resumption in Q1 2021 per Federal Reserve guidance; Board authorization for up to $30B in repurchases.

nodes.title: Common stock
nodes.heading: Common stock
nodes.start_phrase: On March 15, 2020, in response to the economic disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Firm temporarily suspended repurchases of its common stock.
nodes.summary:
- RWA rollforward: Presents changes in Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA) for the three months ended March 31, 2021 under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches. Starts from December 31, 2020 balances and shows impacts from model and data changes, portfolio runoff, and movements in portfolio levels, with definitions of each driver. Results: Standardized total RWA rose to $1,577.0B; Advanced total RWA rose to $1,503.8B.

- Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR): Details components and ratios for March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, including Tier 1 capital, total/adjusted average assets, off-balance sheet exposures, exclusions for U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve deposits, and total leverage exposure. SLR was 6.7% (vs. 6.9% prior); notes SLR excluding temporary relief was 5.5% (vs. 5.8% prior). References bank-level SLR.

- Line of business equity: Shows allocated capital by segment as of March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020: CCB $50.0B, CIB $83.0B, CB $24.0B, AWM $14.0B, Corporate $78.2B; total common stockholders’ equity $249.2B.

- Capital actions:
  - Common dividends: Quarterly dividend of $0.90 per share, subject to Board approval.
  - Common stock: Suspension of buybacks in March 2020 due to COVID-19; Fed-directed halt through end-2020; authorization of up to $30B repurchase program beginning Q1 2021. Fed restrictions tied to average net income limited Q1 2021 distributions; restrictions extended through at least Q2 2021. Q1 2021 repurchases: 34.7M shares for $5.0B (vs. 50.0M shares for $6.4B in Q1 2020).
  - Preferred stock: $379M dividends in Q1 2021; issued $1.5B of 4.55% Series JJ (Mar 17, 2021); announced redemption of $1.4B 6.10% Series AA and $1.2B 6.15% Series BB on June 1, 2021.

Federal Reserve to disclose indicative Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) effective October 1, 2021; current SCB 3.3%. If post-stress minimums are met, temporary distribution restrictions expire June 30, 2021; otherwise could extend through at least September 30, 2021.

- Other capital requirements (TLAC): Outlines Federal Reserve Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity and eligible long-term debt (LTD) minimums, including buffers: TLAC to RWA 22.5% (23.0% at 12/31/20), TLAC to leverage exposure 9.5%, LTD to RWA 9.5%, LTD to leverage exposure 4.5%. Reports eligible amounts and surpluses at March 31, 2021: External TLAC $432.5B (27.4% of RWA; surplus $77.6B) and LTD $188.3B (11.9% of RWA; surplus $38.5B); as a percent of total leverage exposure: TLAC 12.3% (surplus $97.8B) and LTD 5.3% (surplus $29.7B). Notes temporary leverage exposure exclusion for U.S. Treasuries and FRB deposits through March 31, 2021.

- Cross-references: Points to related disclosures in the 2020 Form 10-K and other sections of the Form 10-Q for additional detail on SLR, capital allocation, repurchases, preferred stock, TLAC, liquidity risk management, and resolution-related risk factors.

nodes.title: Preferred stock
nodes.heading: Preferred stock
nodes.start_phrase: Preferred stock dividends declared were $379 million for the three months ended M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Common stock repurchases: For the three months ended March 31, 2021, the firm repurchased 34.7 million shares for $4.999 billion; in the same period of 2020, 50.0 million shares for $6.397 billion. Additional details are referenced in Part II, Item 2 and Item 5 of the Form 10-Q and in the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Preferred stock: Declared $379 million in preferred dividends for Q1 2021. Issued $1.5 billion of 4.55% non-cumulative preferred stock, Series JJ, on March 17, 2021. Announced redemption on June 1, 2021 of $1.4 billion Series AA (6.10%) and $1.2 billion Series BB (6.15%). Further details in Note 17 of the Form 10-Q and Note 21 of the 2020 Form 10-K.

Per the Fed’s March 25, 2021 guidance, if the firm remains above all minimum risk-based capital requirements under the 2021 CCAR results, temporary capital distribution restrictions will expire June 30, 2021; otherwise they continue through at least September 30, 2021. Additional background is in the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity (TLAC) and eligible long-term debt (LTD): The firm is subject to the Federal Reserve’s TLAC rule for U.S. GSIBs. As of March 31, 2021, minimum requirements including buffers: TLAC to RWA 22.5% (was 23.0% at 12/31/20), TLAC to leverage exposure 9.5%, external LTD to RWA 9.5%, external LTD to leverage 4.5%.

nodes.title: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: LIQUIDITY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Liquidity risk is the risk that the Firm will be unable to meet its contractual and contingent financial obligations as they arise or that it does not have the appropriate amount, composition and tenor of funding and liquidity to support its assets and liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (pp. 102–108) and U.S. LCR disclosures for fuller discussion.
- Explains LCR and HQLA: Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must each maintain eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30-day stressed net cash outflows with a minimum LCR of 100%. Excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s HQLA.
- Provides LCR metrics (three-month averages):
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR 110% for Q1 2021 and Q4 2020 (114% in Q1 2020); HQLA in Q1 2021 totaled $696.6B (cash at central banks $578.0B; eligible securities $118.5B); net cash outflows $634.2B; net excess eligible HQLA $62.4B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 166% in Q1 2021 (160% in Q4 2020; 117% in Q1 2020); net excess eligible HQLA $442.6B in Q1 2021.
- Discusses drivers:
  - Firm’s average LCR decreased year-over-year primarily due to higher deposits increasing estimated net cash outflows.
  - Bank’s average LCR increased versus both prior periods due to deposit growth; deposit increases were driven by government actions related to COVID-19. Excess liquidity at the bank is excluded from the Firm’s reported LCR.
  - Notes LCR can fluctuate with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from business activity.
- Details other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities fair value of about $841B at March 31, 2021 (up from $740B at Dec 31, 2020), driven by higher CIB trading assets and increased excess eligible HQLA at the bank from deposit growth.
  - Additional borrowing capacity of approximately $301B at March 31, 2021 ($307B at Dec 31, 2020) at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window based on pledged collateral; this capacity is not viewed as a primary liquidity source and excludes HQLA and other pledged unencumbered securities already at central banks.
- Outlines NSFR:
  - Final U.S. NSFR rule effective July 1, 2021; requires NSFR ≥ 100% on an ongoing basis.
  - Public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will be semi-annual beginning in 2023.
  - The Firm estimates compliance with the 100% NSFR minimum based on its understanding of the final rule.

nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.heading: LCR and HQLA
nodes.start_phrase: The LCR rule requires that the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. maintain an amount of eligible HQLA that is sufficient to meet their respective estimated total net cash outflows over a prospective 30 calendar-day period of significant stress.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and directs readers to the 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for fuller discussion.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain at least 100% LCR; excess HQLA at the bank that isn’t transferable to non‑bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides average LCR metrics for the three months ended March 31, 2021, December 31, 2020, and March 31, 2020:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: LCR 110% (Mar-21 and Dec-20; 114% Mar-20); HQLA composed of eligible cash and securities; net excess eligible HQLA ~$62–66B.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 166% (Mar-21), 160% (Dec-20), 117% (Mar-20); net excess eligible HQLA rose to ~$443B.
- Notes drivers of change:
  - Firm’s YoY LCR decrease due mainly to higher net cash outflows stemming from significant deposit growth.
  - Bank’s LCR increase driven by deposit growth, largely from government actions related to COVID‑19; this excess liquidity at the bank is excluded from the Firm’s LCR.
  - LCR fluctuates with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from business activity.
- Identifies other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities with fair value of ~$841B (Mar-21) vs ~$740B (Dec-20), reflecting higher CIB trading assets and bank excess HQLA from increased deposits.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of ~$301B (Mar-21) vs ~$307B (Dec-20); noted as available but not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- Outlines NSFR:
  - Final U.S. NSFR rule effective July 1, 2021; minimum NSFR of 100%; semiannual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR begins in 2023.
  - The Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% NSFR requirement.

nodes.title: Other liquidity sources
nodes.heading: Other liquidity sources
nodes.start_phrase: In addition to the assets reported in the Firm’s eligible HQLA above, the Firm had unencumbered marketable securities, such as equity and debt securities, that the Firm believes would be available to raise liquidity.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and references JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR Disclosure reports for broader context on the Firm’s Liquidity Risk Management.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must each maintain eligible HQLA sufficient to cover 30-day stressed net cash outflows with a minimum LCR of 100%; surplus HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Provides LCR metrics:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. average LCR: 110% (Q1 2021), 110% (Q4 2020), 114% (Q1 2020).
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. average LCR: 166% (Q1 2021), 160% (Q4 2020), 117% (Q1 2020).
- Details HQLA composition and amounts for the Firm:
  - Eligible cash at central banks: $578.0B (Q1 2021), $455.6B (Q4 2020), $205.0B (Q1 2020).
  - Eligible securities (predominantly U.S. Treasuries, GSE/agency MBS, sovereigns): $118.5B, $241.4B, $343.1B.
  - Total HQLA: $696.6B, $697.1B, $548.2B.
  - Net cash outflows: $634.2B, $634.0B, $482.4B.
  - Net excess eligible HQLA: $62.4B, $63.0B, $65.8B.
  - Bank’s net excess eligible HQLA: $442.6B, $401.9B, $87.1B.
- Notes drivers of changes:
  - Firm’s LCR decreased versus prior year due to higher deposits increasing net cash outflows.
  - Bank’s LCR increased versus both Q4 2020 and Q1 2020 due to deposit growth, largely from government actions related to COVID-19.
  - Excess liquidity at the bank is excluded from the Firm’s LCR under the rule.
  - The Firm’s average LCR fluctuates with changes in HQLA and estimated net cash outflows from ongoing business activity.
- Describes other liquidity sources beyond eligible HQLA:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities with fair value of approximately $841B (Mar 31, 2021) and $740B (Dec 31, 2020); increase driven by higher CIB trading assets and excess eligible HQLA at the bank from deposit growth; actual liquidity raised would depend on market conditions.
  - Available borrowing capacity at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window of about $301B (Mar 31, 2021) and $307B (Dec 31, 2020); excludes benefits from HQLA or other unencumbered securities already pledged; not considered a primary liquidity source.
- Introduces NSFR requirements:
  - Final U.S. NSFR rule (issued Oct 20, 2020) effective July 1, 2021; requires at least 100% NSFR on an ongoing basis.
  - Public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR will be required semi-annually beginning in 2023.
  - The Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% minimum NSFR based on its current understanding of the final rule.

nodes.title: NSFR
nodes.heading: NSFR
nodes.start_phrase: The net stable funding ratio (“NSFR”) is a liquidity requirement for large banking organizations that is intended to measure the adequacy of “available” and “required” amounts of stable funding over a one-year horizon.
nodes.summary:
- Defines liquidity risk and directs readers to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K and U.S. LCR disclosures for more detail.
- Explains LCR and HQLA requirements: both the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must maintain at least 100% LCR; excess HQLA at the bank that is not transferable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported HQLA.
- Summarizes average LCR metrics for the three months ended March 31, 2021, December 31, 2020, and March 31, 2020:
  - Firm: LCR 110% for Mar-21 and Dec-20 (down from 114% in Mar-20); Firm HQLA comprised of eligible cash and securities totaling about $697 billion vs net cash outflows of about $634 billion; net excess eligible HQLA around $62–66 billion.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: LCR 166% (Mar-21), 160% (Dec-20), 117% (Mar-20); net excess eligible HQLA rose to ~$443 billion.
  - Eligible HQLA securities are predominantly U.S. Treasuries, U.S. GSE/agency MBS, and sovereign bonds.
- Describes drivers of changes: deposit growth—largely influenced by government actions related to COVID-19—increased bank liquidity and Firm net cash outflows; bank-level excess liquidity is excluded from Firm LCR.
- Notes that Firm LCR fluctuates with changes in eligible HQLA and estimated net cash outflows due to ongoing business activity.
- Details other liquidity sources:
  - Unencumbered marketable securities of ~$841 billion at Mar-21 (up from ~$740 billion at Dec-20), reflecting higher CIB trading assets and excess HQLA at the bank.
  - Available borrowing capacity of ~$301 billion at FHLBs and the Federal Reserve discount window at Mar-21 (vs ~$307 billion at Dec-20); the discount window is not viewed as a primary liquidity source.
- Introduces the NSFR: final U.S. rule effective July 1, 2021 requires at least 100% NSFR on an ongoing basis, with semi-annual public disclosure of quarterly average NSFR starting in 2023; the Firm estimates it is compliant with the 100% minimum.

nodes.title: Funding
nodes.heading: Funding
nodes.start_phrase: Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
nodes.summary:
- Management asserts sufficient unsecured and secured funding capacity to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
- Diversified funding model:
  - Primary reliance on deposits at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Additional bank funding via short-/long-term secured borrowings, issuance of unsecured long-term debt, and borrowings from the Parent Company or IHC.
  - Non-bank subsidiaries funded mainly by long-term unsecured borrowings and short-term secured borrowings (securities lending/repurchase agreements).
  - Excess funding deployed by Treasury and CIO into investment securities or short-term liquid assets, managed for interest rate and liquidity risk.
- Deposits as a stable funding source:
  - Significant share from consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits tied to client operating relationships, reducing reliance on wholesale markets.
- Deposit levels and trends:
  - Period-end deposits rose to $2.278T at March 31, 2021 from $2.144T at December 31, 2020.
  - Average deposits increased to $2.225T for Q1 2021 from $1.636T for Q1 2020.
  - Growth observed across lines of business (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM), with detailed LOB breakdowns provided.
- Loans and funding mix:
  - Loans were $1.011T at March 31, 2021 (vs. $1.013T at December 31, 2020).
  - Loans-to-deposits ratio declined to 44% from 47%, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loans.
  - Deposits comprised 67% of total liabilities (down from 69% at year-end 2020).
- Drivers of deposit growth:
  - Significant inflows tied to government actions related to COVID-19.
  - In CCB, additional lift from lower consumer spending and growth in both existing and new consumer and small business accounts.
- Methodological note:
  - The Firm views average deposit balances as more representative of trends than period-end balances, though market disruptions can affect patterns.

nodes.title: Sources of funds
nodes.heading: Sources of funds
nodes.start_phrase: Management believes that the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet its on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
nodes.summary:
- Management asserts the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient for on- and off-balance sheet obligations.
- Funding is diversified: primary reliance on deposits at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; additional bank funding via short- or long-term secured borrowings, unsecured long-term debt, and intercompany borrowings (Parent Company or IHC). Non-bank subsidiaries rely mainly on long-term unsecured and short-term secured borrowings (including repos and securities lending).
- Excess funding is deployed by Treasury and CIO into the investment securities portfolio or held in cash/short-term liquid investments based on interest rate and liquidity risk.
- Deposits are a stable funding source; consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits (tied to operating service relationships) are considered especially stable.
- Deposit trends and levels:
  - Total Firm deposits increased to $2.278T at March 31, 2021 (from $2.144T at December 31, 2020).
  - Average deposits for Q1 2021 were $2.225T vs $1.636T in Q1 2020, reflecting broad inflows across LOBs.
  - LOB period-end deposits at March 31, 2021: CCB ~$1.038T; CIB ~$726.7B; Commercial Banking ~$295.7B; Asset & Wealth Management ~$217.5B; Corporate ~$0.3B.
  - Average balances are viewed as more representative over time, though market disruptions can affect trends.
- Loans and ratios:
  - Loans totaled $1.011T at March 31, 2021.
  - Loans-to-deposits ratio declined to 44% (from 47% at December 31, 2020).
  - Deposits were 67% of total liabilities (vs 69% at December 31, 2020).
- Key drivers of deposit growth included government actions related to COVID-19, lower consumer spending, and account growth (notably in CCB).
- Additional detail on deposit and liability trends is referenced in Business Segment Results (pp. 18–34) and Consolidated Balance Sheets Analysis (pp. 12–13).

nodes.title: Deposits
nodes.heading: Deposits
nodes.start_phrase: The table below summarizes, by LOB and Corporate, the period-end deposit balances as of M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2020 , and the average deposit balances for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020 , respectively.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and capacity: Management states the Firm’s unsecured and secured funding capacity is sufficient to meet on- and off-balance sheet obligations. The global balance sheet is funded through diversified sources: stable deposits, secured and unsecured capital markets funding, and stockholders’ equity.

- Entity-level funding mix:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.: Primarily funded by deposits; can also access short- and long-term secured borrowings, issue unsecured long-term debt, or borrow from the Parent Company or IHC.
  - Non-bank subsidiaries: Primarily funded via long-term unsecured borrowings and short-term secured borrowings (notably securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements).
  - Excess funding is invested by Treasury and CIO in investment securities or short-term liquid investments based on rate and liquidity profiles.

- Deposits:
  - Deposits are a stable funding source, with a significant share from consumer deposits and wholesale operating deposits tied to operating service relationships.
  - Period-end deposits rose to $2.278T at March 31, 2021 (from $2.144T at December 31, 2020).
  - By line of business at March 31, 2021: CCB $1.038T; CIB $0.727T; Commercial Banking $0.296T; AWM $0.217T; Corporate $0.0003T.
  - Average deposits for Q1 2021 were $2.225T vs $1.636T in Q1 2020, driven by government actions related to COVID-19, lower spending, and growth in existing/new accounts across consumer and small business customers.
  - Deposits as a percentage of total liabilities: 67% (Mar 31, 2021) vs 69% (Dec 31, 2020).
  - Loans totaled $1.011T, with a loans-to-deposits ratio of 44% (down from 47%).

- Funding excluding deposits (selected balances):
  - Short-term unsecured: $27.6B (Mar 31, 2021) vs $20.5B (Dec 31, 2020); commercial paper increased for short-term liquidity management.
  - Short-term secured: $337.9B vs $248.0B; includes repos ($293.1B vs $207.9B) and securities loaned.
  - Long-term unsecured: $261.9B vs $263.0B; includes senior notes, subordinated debt, and structured notes (some TLAC-eligible).
  - Long-term secured: $21.9B vs $23.6B; components include credit card securitizations and FHLB advances (down).
  - Equity: Preferred stock $31.6B; common stockholders’ equity $249.2B.

- Short-term funding dynamics:
  - Short-term secured funding is primarily repos and securities lending secured by high-quality collateral (U.S. Treasuries, agency/GSE MBS).
  - Repo balances increased due to higher secured financing of AFS investment securities in Treasury and CIO, higher trading assets in CIB, and client activity.
  - Balances in repos/securities lending fluctuate with client investment/financing needs, the Firm’s liability mix management, and market/portfolio factors.
  - Short-term unsecured funding comprises other borrowed funds and commercial paper; commercial paper issuance rose to support liquidity needs.

nodes.title: Short-term funding
nodes.heading: Short-term funding
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s sources of short-term secured funding primarily consist of securities loaned or sold under agreements to repurchase.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s non-deposit funding mix as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, plus average balances for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020.
- Short-term unsecured funding: Comprised of commercial paper and other borrowed funds; increased to $27.6B from $20.5B, driven by higher commercial paper outstanding ($15.2B vs. $12.0B) due to net issuance for short-term liquidity management.
- Short-term secured funding: Dominated by securities sold under repurchase agreements and securities lending; rose to $337.9B from $247.9B, primarily reflecting higher secured financing of available-for-sale investment securities in Treasury and CIO, higher trading assets in CIB, and client activity; balances are variable due to client financing needs, the Firm’s liability mix management, and market/portfolio factors.
- Long-term unsecured funding: Includes senior notes, subordinated debt, and structured notes (some TLAC-eligible); essentially flat at $261.9B vs. $263.0B.
- Long-term secured funding: Includes credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and secured structured notes; declined to $21.9B from $23.6B; average FHLB advances notably lower in Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020 (reflecting reduced reliance on this source).
- Equity: Preferred stock of $31.6B and common stockholders’ equity of $249.2B at March 31, 2021.
- Averages (Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020) highlight mix shifts: short-term secured funding averages higher ($335.1B vs. $271.4B), commercial paper slightly lower on average ($12.9B vs. $14.0B), and FHLB advances markedly lower ($13.7B vs. $27.1B).
- Footnotes and classifications: Repo and securities lending are primarily short-term; certain items are recorded as beneficial interests of consolidated VIEs; “other borrowed funds” include nonrecourse MMLF advances; structured notes include TLAC-eligible debt; references provided to related 10-Q/10-K notes and sections for further detail.

nodes.title: Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.heading: Long-term funding and issuance
nodes.start_phrase: Long-term funding provides an additional source of stable funding and liquidity for the Firm.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: The firm’s long-term funding strategy, composition, issuance activity, and maturities/redemptions for the quarter ended March 31, 2021 (with comparisons to 2020), plus subsequent issuance and secured funding sources.
- Strategy and objectives: Long-term funding supports stable liquidity and regulatory requirements (including TLAC). The plan is driven by client activity, liquidity needs, and regulations, aiming for diversification, broad market access, and optimized costs across markets, tenors, and currencies.
- Issuance structure: The Parent Company issues the significant majority of long-term unsecured funding to support both bank and non-bank subsidiaries; it advances substantially all net proceeds to the IHC. The IHC does not issue debt to external parties. Certain Parent Company issuances are TLAC-eligible.
- Unsecured funding activity (Q1 2021 vs Q1 2020):
  - Parent Company issuance: $13.5bn (vs $9.4bn), primarily senior notes in U.S. ($9.25bn) and non-U.S. ($2.79bn) markets; structured notes $1.5bn; no subordinated debt.
  - Parent Company maturities/redemptions: $4.67bn (vs $6.99bn).
  - Subsidiaries issuance: $10.5bn structured notes (vs $9.25bn); no senior note issuance; no subordinated debt.
  - Subsidiaries maturities/redemptions: $8.58bn (vs $13.45bn); minimal senior note maturities in 2021.
- Subsequent event: After March 31, 2021, the Parent Company issued approximately $16bn of senior notes.
- Secured long-term funding sources: Consumer credit card securitizations, FHLB advances, and other secured long-term funding (including secured structured notes).
  - Issuance: $138mm in Q1 2021 (vs $16.23bn in Q1 2020, driven by $15bn FHLB advances and $1bn credit card securitization).
  - Maturities/redemptions: $1.73bn in Q1 2021 (vs $8.61bn in Q1 2020).
- Scope note: Client-driven loan securitizations in wholesale businesses are excluded as they are not a funding source for the firm.

nodes.title: Credit ratings
nodes.heading: Credit ratings
nodes.start_phrase: The cost and availability of financing are influenced by credit ratings.
nodes.summary:
- Describes how the Firm’s credit ratings affect the cost and availability of financing and liquidity, noting that downgrades could reduce access to liquidity, raise funding costs, trigger additional collateral or funding needs, and limit the pool of willing investors and counterparties.
- States that the impact of downgrades varies with contractual and behavioral factors, which are incorporated into the Firm’s liquidity risk management and stress testing, and asserts the Firm maintains sufficient liquidity to withstand potential funding reductions from downgrades.
- Notes that funding requirements for VIEs and other third-party commitments could be adversely affected by rating declines, with cross-references to sections on SPEs and to Note 4 for details on liquidity risk, credit-related contingent features, derivatives, and collateral agreements.
- Presents the Firm’s and key subsidiaries’ credit ratings as of March 31, 2021 from Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch (showing long-term and short-term ratings with stable outlooks across entities such as JPMorgan Chase & Co., JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and J.P. Morgan Securities).
- Discloses that on April 23, 2021, Fitch affirmed these ratings and revised the outlook to stable.
- Refers readers to the 2020 Form 10-K for additional discussion of factors that could affect the credit ratings of the Parent Company and principal subsidiaries.

nodes.title: CREDIT AND INVESTMENT RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: CREDIT AND INVESTMENT RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Credit and investment risk is the risk associated with the default or change in credit profile of a client, counterparty or customer; or loss of principal or a reduction in expected returns on investments, including consumer credit risk, wholesale credit risk, and investment portfolio risk.
nodes.summary:
- Defines credit and investment risk, covering consumer, wholesale, and investment portfolio risk, and references related sections and JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for detailed frameworks.
- Describes the credit portfolio scope and accounting treatment: loans retained, held-for-sale, and certain loans at fair value (excluding trading assets), with references to notes on loans, commitments, derivatives, investment securities, and securities financing credit risk.
- Presents total credit portfolio data as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, including: loans (reported and by category), derivative receivables, receivables from customers (margin loans), total credit-related assets, assets acquired in loan satisfactions (REO and other), lending-related commitments, and the total credit portfolio.
- Provides credit performance metrics for Q1 2021 vs. Q1 2020: net charge-offs, average retained loans, and net charge-off rates.
- Notes use of credit derivatives for portfolio management (net notional protection purchased/sold) and liquid securities/cash collateral held against derivatives.
- Clarifies treatment of nonperforming assets, excluding certain government-insured mortgages and REO, and notes the policy of generally exempting credit card loans from nonaccrual status.
- Discusses COVID-19-related customer assistance (payment deferrals, covenant modifications), noting most modifications are not TDRs and may delay recognition of delinquencies, nonaccruals, and charge-offs.
- Details the Firm’s participation in the Paycheck Protection Program: application deadline extension, outstanding PPP balances (split between consumer and wholesale), immaterial interest income impact in Q1 2021, and cumulative loan forgiveness processed through March 31, 2021.

nodes.title: CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.heading: CREDIT PORTFOLIO
nodes.start_phrase: Credit risk is the risk associated with the default or change in credit profile of a client, counterparty or customer.
nodes.summary:
- Defines credit and investment risk, covering consumer, wholesale, and investment portfolio risks; points to related sections and 2020 Form 10-K for the broader framework.

nodes.title: Consumer assistance
nodes.heading: Consumer assistance
nodes.start_phrase: In March 2020, the Firm began providing assistance to customers in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, predominantly in the form of payment deferrals.
nodes.summary:
- The Firm launched consumer assistance in March 2020 in response to COVID-19, primarily through payment deferral programs.
- As of March 31, 2021, $9.3 billion of retained loans remained under deferral, down $1.5 billion from December 31, 2020, $3.0 billion from September 30, 2020, and $19.0 billion from June 30, 2020. New Q1 2021 enrollments were approximately $886 million, mainly in residential real estate and credit card.
- Post-deferral performance is strong: predominantly all borrowers exiting deferrals are current. By product (percent of accounts current after exit): residential real estate 96%, auto and other 96%, credit card 94% (note: 89% by balance for credit card). Total consumer: 94%.
- The Firm continues to monitor credit risk during and after deferrals and includes expected losses of principal and accrued interest in its allowance for credit losses.
- Program details and balances by product as of March 31, 2021:
  - Residential real estate: $9.059 billion under deferral (4.1% of class). Rolling three-month deferrals up to 18 months; deferred payments generally due at end of loan term. Weighted average LTV of loans under deferral is 52%. Excludes large volumes of third-party serviced mortgages.
  - Auto and other: $127 million under deferral (0.2% of class). Auto currently offers one-month deferral (initially three), with maturity extended by months deferred. Business Banking offers a three-month deferral with automatic deferment to maturity (loans) or one year forward (lines). Certain risk-rated loans and auto operating leases are excluded; lease deferrals don’t extend term and deferred payments are due at lease end.
  - Credit card: $105 million under deferral (0.1% of class). Currently offers a one-month minimum payment deferral (initially three); interest accrues during the deferral and is added to principal.
  - Total consumer: $9.291 billion under deferral (2.1% of retained consumer loan balances), including $3.6 billion that were TDRs prior to deferral.
- Of the $9.3 billion still under deferral, about $3.9 billion were accounted for as TDRs, either pre-existing or because CARES Act/Consolidated Appropriations Act TDR suspension was not elected or did not apply.
- Most borrowers (including TDRs) were current at enrollment and are expected to exit current, either due to no payments being due during deferral or because deferred payments become due at maturity. Borrowers unable to resume payments will be placed on nonaccrual per policy (except credit cards per regulatory guidance) and charged off or down according to Firm policies.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card

- HFS and FV portfolio: Increased since year-end, mainly from Home Lending warehouse loans; FV nonaccruals decreased due to sales in CIB.
- HELOCs: $22.2B outstanding at March 31, 2021, including $8.6B recast/modified to fully amortizing and $7.3B interest-only balloon HELOCs (mostly maturing after 2030); risk managed by reducing/closing undrawn lines when borrower credit deteriorates.
- Interest-only mortgages: $25.9B at March 31, 2021 (vs. $25.6B at December 31, 2020); typically higher-balance loans to higher-income borrowers, largely in AWM; Q1 2021 charge-offs consistent with the broader residential mortgage portfolio.
- Government-insured/guaranteed mortgages (incl. HFS and FV): $1.719B at March 31, 2021 (current $775M; 30–89 DPD $146M; 90+ DPD $798M) vs. $1.778B at December 31, 2020; allowance considers potential unrecoverable claim exposure.

Excludes short-term/non-concession mods and loans under CARES Act TDR relief. Notes: certain Ginnie Mae repurchased/modified loans are excluded and may be re-sold into pools upon re-performance; $3.0B of TDRs on nonaccrual were less than 90 days past due at both dates.
