nodes.title: Lending-related commitments
nodes.heading: 2.9.5.3.5 Lending-related commitments
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm uses lending-related financial instruments, such as commitments (including revolving credit facilities) and guarantees, to address the financing needs of its clients.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Discussion of the Firm’s credit exposure and risk management across lending-related commitments, customer receivables (margin loans), and derivative contracts.
- Lending-related commitments and guarantees: Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk if drawn or if guarantees are triggered; historically most are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn, so totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs. Refer to Note 22.
- Receivables from customers (margin loans): Held-for-investment margin loans in CIB, CCB, and AWM, collateralized by clients’ brokerage assets (cash and liquid securities). Due to collateralization, no allowance for credit losses is generally recorded. Risk managed via margin requirements, ongoing monitoring, and margin calls or position reductions as needed. Reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable on the Consolidated balance sheets.
- Derivatives purpose and activities: The Firm makes markets in derivatives to help clients manage risks (credit, interest rates, FX, equities, commodities) and uses derivatives to manage its own credit and market risk, including counterparty credit risk from market-making positions.
- Counterparty and settlement credit risk: For OTC derivatives, exposure is to the counterparty; for exchange-traded and OTC-cleared derivatives, exposure can be to central counterparties (CCPs). Credit risk is influenced by counterparty type and settlement mechanism.
- Risk mitigation: Broad use of legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements. Approximately 88% of OTC derivative transactions (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades settled daily) were subject to collateral agreements at both March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020. Refer to Note 4 for collateral and derivative details.
- Derivative receivables and collateral (fair values on the Consolidated balance sheets): $73.1 billion at March 31, 2021 and $79.6 billion at December 31, 2020; decrease driven by market movements.
- Netting and collateral impacts (in millions):
  - Net of cash collateral: $73,119 (Mar 31, 2021) and $79,630 (Dec 31, 2020).
  - Less liquid securities and other cash collateral: $(13,958) and $(14,806), yielding $59,161 and $64,824 net of liquid securities/other cash.
  - Less other collateral: $(5,716) and $(6,022), resulting in total net of collateral of $53,445 and $58,802, respectively.
- Collateral quality and limits: Liquid securities are high quality liquid assets under the LCR rule; other collateral may not qualify as HQLA but is viewed as legally enforceable. Collateral is limited to each counterparty’s net derivative receivable.

nodes.title: Receivables from customers
nodes.heading: 2.9.5.3.6 Receivables from customers
nodes.start_phrase: Receivables from customers reflect held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB and AWM that are collateralized by assets maintained in the clients’ brokerage accounts (e.g., cash on deposit, liquid and readily marketable debt or equity securities).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Discussion of the Firm’s off–balance sheet lending-related commitments, margin loan receivables from customers, and derivative contracts, including credit risk management, collateralization, and period-end derivative receivable balances.

- Lending-related commitments: Includes commitments (e.g., revolving credit facilities) and guarantees. Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk if fully drawn and counterparties default, but historically many are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn; thus, not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs. See Note 22.

- Receivables from customers (margin loans): Held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM, secured by client brokerage assets (cash and liquid, marketable securities). Due to strong collateralization, an allowance for credit losses is generally not recorded. Risk managed via margin requirements, continuous monitoring, and margin calls or position reduction. Reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable.

- Derivative contracts: Used to serve clients’ hedging needs, support market-making, and manage the Firm’s own credit and market risks. Credit exposure varies by counterparty and settlement type: OTC exposes the Firm to counterparties; ETD and OTC-cleared can expose the Firm to CCPs. Risk is mitigated with legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements. Approximately 88% of OTC derivatives (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades) were under collateral agreements at both March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020. See Note 4.

- Derivative receivables and collateral: Fair value of derivative receivables decreased to $73.1B at March 31, 2021 from $79.6B at December 31, 2020, largely due to market movements. Balances are shown net of enforceable netting and cash collateral; additional protection includes liquid securities (HQLA under the LCR rule) and other legally enforceable collateral (non-HQLA). Collateral per counterparty is capped at net exposure.
  - Net of cash collateral: $73.119B (3/31/21) vs $79.630B (12/31/20)
  - Net of liquid securities and other cash collateral: $59.161B vs $64.824B
  - Net of all collateral: $53.445B vs $58.802B
  - Internal ratings profile is referenced.

nodes.title: Derivative contracts
nodes.heading: 2.9.5.3.7 Derivative contracts
nodes.start_phrase: Derivatives enable clients and counterparties to manage risks including credit risk and risks arising from fluctuations in interest rates, foreign exchange, equities, and commodities.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of lending-related commitments and guarantees used to meet client financing needs. Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk if drawn or if guarantees are called and clients default, but historically many commitments are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire undrawn, so totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs (see Note 22).

- Receivables from customers consist of held-for-investment margin loans to brokerage clients in CIB, CCB, and AWM, collateralized by cash and liquid marketable securities in client accounts. Due to collateralization, allowances for credit losses are generally not held. Credit risk is managed via margin requirements and ongoing monitoring, with calls for additional collateral or position reduction as needed. Reported within accrued interest and accounts receivable.

- Derivative contracts: the Firm makes markets and uses derivatives to manage client and Firm risks (credit, interest rate, FX, equity, commodity) and associated counterparty credit risk. Credit exposure varies by counterparty type and settlement mechanism (OTC vs exchange-traded/cleared), with risk to counterparties or CCPs. Credit risk mitigation through legally enforceable master netting and collateral agreements. Approximately 88% of OTC derivatives (excluding FX spot and centrally cleared trades) are subject to collateral agreements at March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020 (see Note 4).

- Derivative receivables and collateral:
  - Fair value of derivative receivables: $73.1B at March 31, 2021 vs $79.6B at December 31, 2020, primarily lower in CIB due to market movements.
  - Net derivative receivables after cash collateral: $73,119M (Mar-21) vs $79,630M (Dec-20).
  - Less liquid securities and other cash collateral: $(13,958)M vs $(14,806)M.
  - Net of liquid securities and other cash collateral: $59,161M vs $64,824M.
  - Less other collateral: $(5,716)M vs $(6,022)M.
  - Total net of all collateral: $53,445M vs $58,802M.
  - Additional collateral (e.g., cash, G7 and other liquid government/agency securities, corporate debt/equity) posted at initiation, for non-daily calls, or pending return does not reduce reported balances but is available as security.

- Ratings profile of derivative receivables net of collateral:
  - Investment-grade: $32,774M (61%) at Mar-21 vs $37,013M (63%) at Dec-20.
  - Noninvestment-grade: $20,671M (39%) at Mar-21 vs $21,789M (37%) at Dec-20.

- Credit derivatives:
  - Used both for market-making and, as an end-user, for credit portfolio management to mitigate credit risk on loans, lending-related commitments, and derivatives counterparty exposure.
  - Net notional protection in credit portfolio management:
    - Loans and lending-related commitments: $2,161M (Mar-21) vs $3,877M (Dec-20).
    - Derivative receivables: $20,488M vs $18,362M.
    - Total: $22,649M vs $22,239M.
  - Additional detail and definitions referenced to Note 4 (Form 10-Q) and Note 5 (2020 Form 10-K).

nodes.title: ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.heading: 2.9.5.4 ALLOWANCE FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain o ff-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and definition: Describes the Firm’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off‑balance sheet lending commitments. Breaks down ACL into: allowance for loan losses (scored and risk‑rated retained loans), allowance for lending‑related commitments, and allowance for credit losses on HTM and AFS investment securities.

- Change in allowance (Q1 2021 vs. Dec 31, 2020): Overall ACL decreased, driven by:
  - $4.5 billion reduction in consumer, predominantly credit cards, and residential real estate (benefiting from improved home price index expectations and portfolio runoff).
  - $716 million net reduction in wholesale across lines of business, reflecting improved macroeconomic scenarios.

- Modeling, COVID-19 impacts, and management judgment: Notes pandemic-driven stress on macroeconomic variables (MEVs) used in models, limitations when MEVs fall outside historical training ranges, and continued reliance on management overlays/adjustments. Although conditions improved, uncertainties persist (labor market health, vaccine efficacy vs. variants, potential lasting shifts in consumer behavior and sector impacts).

- Scenario weighting and outlook: Significant weighting retained on adverse scenarios, implying weighted average U.S. unemployment above 8% in 2021 and around 6% into Q2 2022; U.S. GDP expected to return to pre‑pandemic levels in Q1 2022.

- Central case macro assumptions:
  - As of March 31, 2021: U.S. unemployment (avg) 5.7% in Q2’21, 4.8% in Q4’21, 4.3% in Q2’22; cumulative change in real GDP from 12/31/2019 of 0.2%, 2.7%, and 4.3%, respectively.
  - As of December 31, 2020: U.S. unemployment 6.8%, 5.7%, 5.1%; cumulative GDP change (1.9)%, 0.6%, 2.0%. Subsequent forecast changes will flow through future provisions.

- Cross‑references: Points to 2020 Form 10‑K Notes 13 and 10 for methodologies and judgments; Critical Accounting Estimates (pp. 74–76); Consumer and Wholesale Credit Portfolio sections and Note 11 for more detail.

- Quantitative details (three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020):
  - Loan loss allowance activity by segment (consumer ex‑card, credit card, wholesale): beginning balances, charge‑offs/recoveries, net charge‑offs, provisions (notably negative in Q1’21, indicating reserve releases), ending balances.
  - Lending‑related commitments allowance: beginning balances, provisions, ending balances.
  - Ending total ACL (loans plus lending commitments) of $25.5 billion at March 31, 2021 (excludes HTM securities allowance; HTM ACL was $94 million at March 31, 2021 vs. $19 million at March 31, 2020).
  - Impairment methodology split: asset‑specific vs. portfolio‑based, with the majority portfolio‑based.
  - Memo: retained loans (end‑of‑period and average) and key credit ratios (allowance to loans by segment, allowance to nonaccrual loans, and net charge‑off rates). Notes policy generally exempts credit card loans from nonaccrual status.

nodes.title: INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.9.5.5 INVESTMENT PORTFOLIO RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Investment portfolio risk is the risk associated with the loss of principal or a reduction in expected returns on investments arising from the investment securities portfolio or from principal investments.
nodes.summary:
- Defines investment portfolio risk as potential loss of principal or reduced returns arising from the Firm’s investment securities portfolio and principal investments. Securities are predominantly held by Treasury and CIO for balance sheet and asset-liability management; principal investments are privately held, non-traded, managed within LOBs and Corporate, and intended for long-term holding with no expectation of short-term gains.
- Investment securities risk centers on default risk (principal and interest), mitigated by a high-quality portfolio. As of March 31, 2021, Treasury and CIO held $595.4 billion (net of allowance for credit losses) with an average AA+ rating (based on external or, if unavailable, internal ratings). Cross-references are provided to Corporate segment results, Note 9, Market Risk Management, and Liquidity Risk Management for details.
- Principal investment risk covers privately held junior capital across multiple asset classes, made by dedicated investing businesses or as part of broader strategies. These include tax-oriented investments and strategic investments that support underserved communities and minority-owned businesses. Managed by LOBs and Corporate; aggregate carrying values were not significantly affected by COVID-19, though uncertainty remains.
- Aggregate carrying values (in billions): March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020—tax-oriented investments $19.5 vs. $20.0; private equity/various debt and equity/real assets $5.8 vs. $6.2; total $25.3 vs. $26.2. Prior-period amounts were revised (see Note 1).
- Governance and oversight of Investment Portfolio Risk Management are referenced to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K, page 134.

nodes.title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.9.6 MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held for both the short and long term.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as the impact of changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities on asset and liability values.
- Notes ongoing monitoring of COVID-19 impacts on market risk using established measures and controls.
- Emphasizes inherent model imprecision, especially during sudden market shifts (e.g., early COVID-19), and references broader model risk governance.
- Describes periodic review, enhancement, and calibration of market risk measures to reflect portfolio and market changes.
- Outlines a single VaR framework supporting both Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Details Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss methodology approximating a 95% confidence level, aligned to daily risk management decisions.
- Details Regulatory VaR: daily aggregated measure per regulatory rules used for Basel III regulatory capital requirements.
- Notes that VaR models are periodically evaluated and enhanced, which may affect historical comparability.
- Provides references for further details: 2020 Form 10-K sections on Market Risk Management, VaR limitations and differences between Risk Management and Regulatory VaR, model reviews/approvals, nonstatistical risk measures, and Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures (including stressed VaR and backtesting).

nodes.title: Value-at-risk
nodes.heading: 2.9.6.1 Value-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse market moves in the current market environment.
nodes.summary:
- Defines market risk as exposure to changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities affecting asset and liability values.
- Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for detailed discussions on market risk organization, measurement, monitoring and control, and activities that drive market risk, as well as other risk measures and model risk governance.
- Notes active monitoring of COVID-19 impacts on market risk using existing measures and controls, and highlights model uncertainty heightened by sudden market shifts.
- Describes ongoing review and calibration of market risk measures in response to portfolio composition, market conditions, and modeling improvements.
- Explains the Firm’s single VaR framework supporting both Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Risk Management VaR: one-day holding period, expected tail-loss approach approximating a 95% confidence level; intended to align with day-to-day risk management decisions.
- Regulatory VaR: separately calculated under regulatory rules and used for Basel III market risk capital requirements; references to Pillar 3 disclosures for VaR, stressed VaR, and backtesting.
- Acknowledges VaR model limitations and potential changes that may affect historical comparability; references to Form 10-K for inherent limitations and differences between Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
- Presents detailed VaR results (average, minimum, maximum) for Q1 2021, Q4 2020, and Q1 2020 by risk type (fixed income, FX, equities, commodities) and by portfolio (CIB trading, credit portfolio, CCB, Corporate/other LOB), including diversification benefits.
- Highlights a specific driver: elevated Corporate/other LOB VaR in late 2020 and early 2021 due to a private equity position that became publicly traded; position exited by March 31, 2021.
- Quarter-over-quarter: average total VaR up $10 million in Q1 2021 vs Q4 2020, mainly from higher fixed income exposure; partially offset as extreme March 2020 COVID-19 volatility rolled out of the one-year look-back.
- Year-over-year: average total VaR up $47 million vs Q1 2020, driven by COVID-19-related volatility (particularly fixed income) and the Corporate VaR impact from the public equity position; partly offset by equities risk reductions.
- Methodology refinement effective July 1, 2020: excluded certain asset-backed FVO loans from VaR into other sensitivity-based measures; without this change, reported average VaR would have been higher (e.g., Total VaR +$18 million in Q1 2021).
- Notes trend of daily Risk Management VaR over five trailing quarters, with declines by March 31, 2021 as March 2020 volatility rolls off.
- Describes daily VaR backtesting approach and revenue components excluded for backtesting purposes per Basel III rules.
- Backtesting results: over 12 months ended March 31, 2021, 165/259 days with gains and two exceptions; over three months ended March 31, 2021, 47/63 days with gains and no exceptions.
- Provides distribution of daily backtesting gains/losses relative to VaR and explains definition of backtesting exceptions; notes differences between Risk Management VaR backtesting here and Regulatory VaR backtesting in Pillar 3 disclosures.

nodes.title: VaR backtesting
nodes.heading: 2.9.6.2 VaR backtesting
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting , which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes.
nodes.summary:
- Presents daily Risk Management VaR across five trailing quarters (Q1 2020–Q1 2021). Average total VaR rose by $47 million for the quarter ended March 31, 2021 versus the prior-year quarter, but daily VaR as of March 31, 2021 declined from March 31, 2020 as the extreme March 2020 COVID-19 volatility rolled out of the one-year look-back window.
- Describes VaR backtesting methodology: compares daily Risk Management VaR to daily backtesting gains/losses; backtesting P&L excludes intraday client-driven trading and intraday risk management activities, fees, commissions, certain valuation adjustments, and net interest income; approach aligns with Basel III backtesting requirements, and excluded items may offset backtesting P&L.
- Backtesting results: over the 12 months ended March 31, 2021, gains on 165 of 259 days with two VaR exceptions; over the three months ended March 31, 2021, gains on 47 of 63 days with no exceptions.
- Explains distribution chart of firmwide daily backtesting gains/losses for the trailing 12 months and three months ended March 31, 2021: losses shown as a percentage of daily VaR, counts grouped in 50-percentage-point intervals; exceptions occur when daily loss exceeds prior-day VaR and appear in intervals above 100%. Notes these results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Market Risk disclosures, which use Regulatory VaR on covered positions.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
nodes.heading: 2.9.6.3 Earnings-at-risk
nodes.start_phrase: The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported net income is important as interest rate risk represents one of the Firm’s significant market risks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: JPMorgan Chase’s management of interest rate risk via earnings-at-risk (EaR), a key market risk affecting reported net income.
- Scope of exposure: Arises from trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance) and the investment securities portfolio; positions by line of business and Corporate are summarized in the 2020 Form 10-K.
- EaR definition: Estimates sensitivity of net interest income plus certain interest-sensitive fees over the next 12 months relative to a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
- Methodology: Simulations cover U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures and include retained loans, deposits, deposits with banks, investment securities, long-term debt, related interest rate hedges, and funds transfer pricing; linked to VaR and other sensitivity measures.
- Scenario design:
  - Parallel shift: equal changes to short- and long-term rates.
  - Steeper curve: long-term rates up, short-term rates unchanged.
  - Flatter curve: short-term rates up, long-term rates unchanged.
- Key assumptions: Instantaneous rate shocks; forecasted balance sheet; modeled prepayment/reinvestment behavior; deposit betas (pricing sensitivity with potential lags); excludes assumed management or client actions. Mortgage prepayment modeling reflects rate differentials, loan seasoning, and historical experience.
- Model governance: Scenarios and models are periodically refined for balance sheet changes, market conditions, and simulation improvements; EaR is not a forecast of net interest income.
- U.S. dollar sensitivities (in billions):
  - +100 bps parallel: $6.0 (Mar 31, 2021) vs $6.9 (Dec 31, 2020).
  - +100 bps steeper (long-term up): $1.6 vs $2.4.
  - +100 bps flatter (short-term up): $4.4 vs $4.5.
  - Changes reflect higher long-term rate baseline and balance sheet shifts; sensitivity driven by assets repricing faster than deposits.
- Negative rates: A downward parallel shift up to 100 bps would reduce net interest income; modeling under negative rates requires additional management judgment; the U.S. has not experienced negative Fed policy rates.
- Non-U.S. dollar sensitivities (in billions):
  - +100 bps parallel: $0.9 in both periods.
  - +100 bps flatter (short-term up): $0.9 vs $0.8.
  - Steeper curve scenario impact not material in either period.

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.heading: 2.9.6.4 Other sensitivity-based measures
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm quantifies the market risk of certain debt and equity and funding activities by assessing the potential impact on net revenue, other comprehensive income (“OCI”) and noninterest expense due to changes in relevant market variables.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: “Other sensitivity-based measures” used by JPMorgan Chase to quantify market risk for certain debt, equity, and funding activities that are outside VaR and earnings-at-risk, showing potential impacts on net revenue, OCI, and noninterest expense from specified market shocks.
- Scope of positions:
  - Debt and equity not in VaR/EaR:
    - Asset Management activities: seed capital and hedges, fund co-investments, and certain deferred compensation and related hedges.
    - Other debt and equity: certain asset-backed loans elected at fair value, privately held equity, and other fair value investments.
  - Funding activities:
    - Non-USD long-term debt (LTD) hedges: cross-currency basis risk and FX revaluation of hedges.
    - Derivatives funding spread risk (FVA).
    - Fair value option (FVO) liabilities: funding spread risk (DVA) and own-credit spread–related interest rate sensitivity, plus related risk-management positions.
- Methodology:
  - Simple shocks applied, with hedging instruments presented net of hedged positions.
  - Key shocks include: 10% changes in market values or FX rates; 1 basis point parallel changes in cross-currency basis or spreads.
  - Sensitivities are illustrative, not predictions, and may differ from realized results due to varying movements across maturities.
- Key quantitative indications (March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020):
  - 10% decline in Asset Management-related market values: ~$(51)m vs $(48)m.
  - 10% decline in Other debt and equity: ~$(885)m vs $(919)m.
  - 1 bp tightening in non-USD LTD cross-currency basis: ~$(17)m vs $(16)m (OCI).
  - 10% FX depreciation on non-USD LTD hedges: ~$17m vs $13m (OCI).
  - 1 bp increase in derivatives funding spread (FVA): ~$(3)m vs $(4)m (net revenue).
  - 1 bp increase in FVO liabilities spread (DVA): ~$39m vs $33m (OCI).
  - Own-credit spread IR sensitivity on FVO liabilities: ~$(1)m vs $(3)m (OCI), partly offset by related risk-management positions: ~$1m vs $3m (net revenue).
- Reporting notes:
  - Equities measured under the measurement alternative are excluded.
  - Impact classification: net revenue (b), noninterest expense (c), OCI (d).
  - Reference to 2020 Form 10-K (page 136) for underlying business activities.

nodes.title: COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.9.7 COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm, through its LOBs and Corporate, may be exposed to country risk resulting from financial, economic, political or other significant developments which adversely affect the value of the Firm’s exposures related to a particular country or set of countries.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the Firm’s Country Risk Management (CRM) approach: monitoring financial, economic, political, and other developments by country; assessing diversification versus strategy and risk tolerance; continued focus on COVID-19 impacts by country.
- References additional detail in JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (pages 143–144).
- Presents risk reporting of the Firm’s top 20 non-U.S. country exposures as of March 31, 2021, with comparisons to December 31, 2020; notes that selections reflect largest exposures under the Firm’s internal approach and are not signals of adverse credit views; exposures fluctuate with client activity and market flows.
- Highlights a notable change: a significant increase in Australia exposure, driven by higher cash placements with the country’s central bank following policy decisions and growth in client deposits.
- Summarizes largest exposures: Germany, United Kingdom, and Japan lead overall; other key countries include Australia, France, China, Switzerland, Brazil, Canada, and Luxembourg.
- Defines exposure categories:
  - Lending and deposits: loans and accrued interest, lending commitments (net of eligible collateral and allowance for credit losses), deposits with banks/central banks, acceptances, other monetary assets, and letters of credit (net of participations); excludes intraday/operational settlement and clearing exposures.
  - Trading and investing: market-making inventory, investment securities, and counterparty exposure on derivatives and securities financing (net of eligible collateral and hedging), including single-name and index exposures tied to listed countries.
  - Other: predominantly physical commodity inventory.
- Notes coverage: the table captures 89% (Mar 31, 2021) and 90% (Dec 31, 2020) of firmwide non-U.S. exposure attributable to specific countries.
- Clarifies that December 31, 2020 figures are displayed using the March 31, 2021 country ranking order.

nodes.title: Risk Reporting
nodes.heading: 2.9.7.1 Risk Reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents the Firm’s top 20 exposures by country (excluding the U.S.) as of M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 and their comparative exposures as of D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0.
nodes.summary:
- Explains JPMorgan Chase’s approach to country risk management: the Firm’s LOBs and Corporate can face financial, economic, political, or other country-specific risks; the Country Risk Management group monitors portfolios, assesses diversification, and aligns exposures with strategy and risk tolerance.
- Notes continued monitoring of COVID-19 impacts on individual countries and references the 2020 Form 10-K (pp. 143–144) for more detail.
- Provides risk reporting via a table of the top 20 non-U.S. country exposures as of March 31, 2021 (with December 31, 2020 comparatives), emphasizing that selection reflects largest exposures under the Firm’s internal approach and is not an indication of adverse credit conditions; exposures can fluctuate with client activity and market flows.
- Highlights a notable increase in Australia exposure to $31.2B, driven by higher cash placements with the Reserve Bank of Australia following policy decisions and growth in client deposits.
- Identifies largest exposures: Germany (largest), United Kingdom, Japan, and Australia among the top; some countries (e.g., China, Switzerland, Italy) show declines versus year-end while others (e.g., Japan, Brazil) increased.
- Breaks down exposures into:
  - Lending and deposits: loans and accrued interest, lending commitments (net of eligible collateral and ACL), deposits with banks/central banks, acceptances, other monetary assets, and letters of credit net of participations; excludes intraday/operating settlement and clearing exposures.
  - Trading and investing: market-making inventory, investment securities, and counterparty exposure on derivatives and securities financing, net of eligible collateral and hedging; includes single-name and index exposures tied to listed countries.
  - Other: predominantly physical commodity inventory.
- Notes coverage: table represents 89%–90% of total Firmwide non-U.S. exposure attributable to individual countries; December 31, 2020 figures are shown in the March 31, 2021 country ranking order.

nodes.title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.9.8 OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems; human factors; or external events impacting the Firm’s processes or systems; Operational Risk includes compliance, conduct, legal, and estimations and model risk.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed processes/systems, human factors, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risks.
- Notes operational risk is inherent to the Firm’s activities and can appear via fraud, business interruptions, cyberattacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, or vendor failures.
- States the objective of Operational Risk Management is to manage risk at appropriate levels relative to the Firm’s financial position, business profile, and regulatory/market environments; references detailed discussion in JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (pages 145–147).
- Highlights subcategories—Compliance, Conduct, Legal, and Estimations and Model risk—captured through operational risk measurement processes; points to 10-K pages 148–151 for more information.
- Details business and technology resiliency risk: disruptions from pandemics, severe weather, utility outages, third-party failures, cyberattacks, flooding, strikes, terrorism, and health emergencies; emphasizes employee and customer safety and a firmwide resiliency program with governance, training, testing, and strategic/tactical initiatives that have sustained operations through events.
- Describes heightened cybersecurity risk due to increased remote work and third-party video conferencing during COVID-19, with added precautionary measures deployed.
- Notes elevated payment fraud risk during COVID-19 driven by alternative authentication methods and pandemic-related scams, with evolving tactics; the Firm applies controls and enhances employee/client education and awareness.

nodes.title: Subcategories and examples of operational risks
nodes.heading: 2.9.8.1 Subcategories and examples of operational risks
nodes.start_phrase: Operational risk can manifest itself in various ways.
nodes.summary:
- Defines operational risk as losses from failed internal processes/systems, human error, or external events, encompassing compliance, conduct, legal, and estimations/model risk.
- Notes operational risk is inherent in the Firm’s activities and can appear via fraud, business interruptions, cyberattacks, employee misconduct, regulatory noncompliance, and vendor failures.
- States the Firm manages operational risk relative to its financial position, business characteristics, and market/regulatory environments, with references to detailed discussions in JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (pages 145–151).
- Highlights subcategories (Compliance, Conduct, Legal, Estimations and Model risk) and that associated losses are captured through operational risk measurement processes.
- Details business and technology resiliency risk and the Firmwide resiliency program, including governance, training, testing, and initiatives to maintain critical operations and protect employees and customers during disruptions (e.g., pandemics, severe weather, power/telecom outages, third-party failures, cyber events, strikes, terrorism, health emergencies).
- Notes heightened cybersecurity focus during COVID-19 due to increased remote access and third-party video conferencing, with added precautionary controls deployed.
- Describes elevated payment fraud risk during the pandemic, driven by alternative authentication methods and scams, and the Firm’s response via controls and employee/client education and awareness programs.

nodes.title: ESTIMATIONS AND MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.heading: 2.9.9 ESTIMATIONS AND MODEL RISK MANAGEMENT
nodes.start_phrase: Estimations and Model risk, a subcategory of operational risk, is the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused estimation outputs.
nodes.summary:
- Defines estimation and model risk as a form of operational risk arising from incorrect or misused estimation outputs.
- Notes widespread use of models and judgment-based estimations across the Firm for valuation, risk measurement, regulatory capital, stress testing, and business decisions, with varying sophistication.
- Emphasizes inherent model imprecision, which can be amplified by market or economic conditions that differ from historical data used to train models (e.g., COVID-19 impacts).
- Highlights the resulting need for increased judgment and analytical overlays to adjust model outputs during atypical periods.
- Directs readers to related disclosures for further detail: Critical Accounting Estimates (pp. 74–76), Note 2 of the Form 10-Q, and the Estimations and Model Risk Management section of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (p. 151).

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.heading: 2.10 CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase ’s accounting policies and use of estimates are integral to understanding its reported results.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates with a focus on its allowance for credit losses. It emphasizes the firm’s governance: well-controlled, independently reviewed, and consistently applied estimation methodologies, with structured processes for any methodology changes. The allowance for credit losses is estimated over the remaining expected life of applicable assets and comprises the allowance for loan losses (scored and risk-rated portfolios), lending-related commitments, and credit losses on HTM and AFS securities.

Key judgments include macroeconomic forecasting and weighting, incorporation of historical loss experience, assessment of portfolio risk characteristics, risk ratings, collateral valuation, and determination of remaining expected life. The firm uses an eight-quarter forecast incorporating hundreds of macroeconomic variables, with modeled losses primarily driven by fewer than twenty. For consumer portfolios, key variables include U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), and real GDP; for wholesale, U.S. real GDP, unemployment, equity prices, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI.

The firm notes significant uncertainty and sensitivity of allowances to changes in assumptions, particularly amid COVID-19-driven weaknesses and ongoing uncertainties around labor market health, vaccine effectiveness against variants, and potential structural shifts in consumer behavior. It highlights that inputs may change at different rates and in offsetting directions, complicating isolation of individual effects.

A scenario comparison illustrates sensitivity: relative to the central scenario, the adverse scenario assumes materially higher U.S. unemployment (average +2.4 percentage points over eight quarters; peak +4.4 points in Q3 2021), lower real GDP (2.6% lower by the end; peak gap 6.6% in Q3 2021), and a lower national HPI (peak difference 17.4%, trough in Q2 2022). The firm concludes that changes in economic assumptions could significantly impact the allowance from period to period.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses
nodes.heading: 2.10.1 Allowance for credit losses
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management’s estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm’s financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates, emphasizing governance: well-controlled, independently reviewed, consistently applied methodologies, and controlled processes for changing methods.
- Allowance for credit losses: management’s estimate of expected lifetime losses for amortized-cost assets and certain off-balance sheet commitments; composed of (1) allowance for loan losses (scored and risk-rated portfolios), (2) allowance for lending-related commitments, and (3) allowance for credit losses on HTM and AFS investment securities.
- Key judgments in the allowance include macroeconomic forecast development and weighting, use of historical loss experience, assessment of portfolio risk characteristics and ratings, collateral valuation, and determination of remaining expected life; references provided to related 10-K/10-Q notes.
- Eight-quarter forecast framework uses hundreds of macroeconomic variables (MEVs), with losses driven primarily by fewer than 20; key MEVs: consumer—U.S. unemployment, home price index (HPI), real GDP; wholesale—U.S. real GDP, unemployment, equity prices, corporate credit spreads, oil prices, commercial real estate prices, and HPI.
- COVID-19 impacts: stressed labor markets and borrowers across consumer and wholesale portfolios; persistent uncertainty around labor market health, vaccine efficacy vs. variants, and potential behavioral shifts affecting sectors; acknowledges difficulty isolating effects of single inputs due to interrelated, nonlinear MEVs and heterogeneous impacts across geographies/products.
- Sensitivity illustration (as of March 31, 2021): comparison of modeled losses under a “central” vs. “relative adverse” scenario over eight quarters. Relative adverse assumes: U.S. unemployment averaging 2.4% higher (peak +4.4% in Q3 2021); lower real GDP (ending 2.6% below, peak difference 6.6% in Q3 2021); and lower national HPI (peak difference 17.4%, trough in Q2 2022).
- Modeled incremental loss differences (relative adverse vs. central), excluding qualitative offsets and additional adverse weighting already applied: +$0.7B residential real estate loans/commitments; +$3.6B credit card loans; +$2.1B wholesale loans/commitments. Notes substantial limitations and that results do not directly translate to changes in the overall allowance.
- Management asserts allowance estimates were reasonable and appropriate as of March 31, 2021.
- Fair value measurements: significant portion of assets/liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis (derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing) and on a nonrecurring basis (certain loans measured via collateral).
- Fair value profile at March 31, 2021 (assets): total at fair value $1,365.4B, of which Level 3 $18.1B; total firm assets $3,689.3B; Level 3 equals 0.5% of total firm assets and 1.3% of assets at fair value. Category highlights (Level 3): trading—debt/equity $2.7B; derivative receivables $7.9B; loans $1.8B; mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) $4.5B; “Other” $0.5B; recurring Level 3 total $17.4B; nonrecurring Level 3 $0.7B. Footnote clarifies derivative Level 3 amounts shown before netting/collateral effects for valuation transparency.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.heading: 2.10.2 Fair value
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase carries a portion of its assets and liabilities at fair value.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and caveats of credit loss analysis: The firm emphasizes that the sensitivity analysis is not a forecast of future allowance changes due to heavy weighting of adverse scenarios already embedded in the allowance, the nonlinear and interrelated effects of macroeconomic variables (MEVs), unprecedented COVID-19 impacts creating higher model uncertainty, and potential shifts in pandemic severity, policy support, and recovery trajectory that could materially affect expected losses beyond modeled sensitivities.
- Scenario comparison as of March 31, 2021: Comparing modeled results under an adverse scenario to a central scenario (without additional adverse weighting or qualitative offsets) indicates approximate increases in expected credit losses of $0.7 billion for residential real estate loans and commitments, $3.6 billion for credit card loans, and $2.1 billion for wholesale loans and commitments.
- Limitations of modeled outputs: The sensitivity results relate only to modeled lifetime loss estimates and exclude qualitative adjustments and management judgment that could alter the overall allowance.
- Governance and reasonableness: Despite macroeconomic uncertainty, the firm asserts that its governance over forecasting and allowance estimation is appropriate and that estimates as of March 31, 2021 were reasonable.
- Fair value disclosures: JPMorgan Chase measures portions of assets and liabilities at fair value on recurring (e.g., derivatives, structured notes, certain securities financing) and nonrecurring bases (e.g., certain mortgage, home equity, and other loans based on collateral).
- Fair value composition and Level 3 detail (March 31, 2021): 
  - Total assets measured at fair value: $1,365.4 billion, including $1,362.9 billion recurring and $2.5 billion nonrecurring.
  - Total Level 3 assets at fair value: $18.1 billion; 0.5% of total firm assets ($3,689.3 billion) and 1.3% of total assets at fair value.
  - Key line items at fair value (Level 3 where applicable): Trading assets $544.0 billion (Level 3: $10.6 billion, including $7.9 billion derivative receivables), AFS securities $379.9 billion (no Level 3), Loans $50.8 billion (Level 3: $1.8 billion), MSRs $4.5 billion (all Level 3), Other $383.7 billion (Level 3: $0.5 billion).
  - Footnote: Level 3 derivative receivables exclude netting adjustments for valuation transparency; applying netting (including cash collateral) would reduce reported Level 3 balances.

nodes.title: Valuation
nodes.heading: 2.10.3 Valuation
nodes.start_phrase: Estimating fair value requires the application of judgment.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on the significant management judgment required to estimate fair value, especially for Level 3 instruments that rely on unobservable inputs and internal valuation models.
- Description of the valuation process: selecting appropriate models/techniques, deriving inputs from empirical data (e.g., yield curves, interest rates, prepayment/default rates, volatilities, correlations, market prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, credit curves), and applying valuation adjustments for Levels 2 and 3 (counterparty and own credit, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio size).
- Acknowledgment that market volatility and illiquidity increase valuation uncertainty and the range of reasonable estimates; different methodologies or assumptions could produce different fair values.
- Reference to Note 2 for detailed valuation hierarchy, processes, unobservable inputs, and adjustments.
- Goodwill impairment testing requires significant judgment, with goodwill allocated to reporting units; references provided to prior filings and Note 14 for the March 31, 2021 assessment.
- Credit card rewards liability disclosed at $8.0 billion (March 31, 2021) and $7.7 billion (December 31, 2020), recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities; assumptions and sensitivities referenced to prior filings.
- Income tax accounting involves significant assumptions and judgments; details referenced to prior filings.
- Litigation reserves rely on significant estimates and judgments; additional information referenced to current and prior filings.

nodes.title: Goodwill impairment
nodes.heading: 2.10.4 Goodwill impairment
nodes.start_phrase: Management applies significant judgment when testing goodwill for impairment.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s critical accounting estimates and judgments. It emphasizes the valuation of financial instruments, noting that fair value estimation relies on management judgment that increases as market observability decreases, particularly for Level 3 instruments. Management selects appropriate valuation models and derives significant unobservable inputs (e.g., yield curves, rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, market prices, FX rates, credit curves), and applies valuation adjustments for Levels 2 and 3 to reflect counterparty credit, the Firm’s creditworthiness, funding, liquidity, unobservable parameters, and portfolio size. It highlights that market volatility can widen reasonable valuation ranges, imprecision can affect reported gains and losses, and differing methodologies could yield different fair values, with further details referenced in Note 2. The section also covers goodwill impairment testing, noting significant judgment in allocating goodwill to reporting units and referring to the 2020 Form 10-K and Note 14 for the March 31, 2021 assessment. It discloses the credit card rewards liability of $8.0 billion at March 31, 2021 ($7.7 billion at December 31, 2020), recorded in accounts payable and other liabilities, with assumptions and sensitivities detailed in the 2020 Form 10-K. Finally, it references the 2020 Form 10-K for significant judgments in accounting for income taxes and points to Note 24 of the Form 10-Q and Note 30 of the 10-K for litigation reserve estimates.

nodes.summary:

Management selects appropriate valuation models and derives inputs from empirical data such as yield curves, interest rates, prepayment speeds, default rates, volatilities, correlations, market prices, comparable valuations, FX rates, and credit curves.

- Acknowledgment that imprecision in unobservable inputs can affect gains and losses; valuation methods may vary across businesses; alternative methodologies or assumptions could yield different fair values. References to Note 2 for detailed valuation process, hierarchy, and adjustments.

nodes.title: ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.heading: ACCOUNTING AND REPORTING DEVELOPMENTS
nodes.start_phrase: •Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Accounting and reporting developments—FASB standards adopted since January 1, 2021.
- Standard covered: Reference Rate Reform (issued March 2020; updated January 2021).
- Key guidance: Optional expedients/exceptions for contracts, financial instruments, and hedge accounting affected by reference rate changes.
- Elections allowed:
  - Treat certain contract amendments as modifications rather than extinguishments.
  - Permit changes to critical hedge terms without automatically terminating hedge relationships.
  - One-time option to transfer securities out of held-to-maturity if criteria are met.
  - January 2021 update: treat derivatives modified for discounting, margining, or contract price alignment (“discounting transition”) as modifications.
- Effective dates: March 12, 2020 for the original standard; January 7, 2021 for the update.
- Company adoption: Applied select expedients for contract modifications, hedge accounting, and discounting transition beginning Q3 2020; discounting transition applied retrospectively.
- Impact: Elections aimed at reducing administrative burden; no material impact on the Consolidated Financial Statements.

nodes.title: Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.heading: Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Standards Adopted since January 1, 2021
nodes.start_phrase: •Provides optional expedients and exceptions to current accounting guidance when financial instruments, hedge accounting relationships, and other transactions are amended due to reference rate reform.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines FASB’s Reference Rate Reform standards adopted since January 1, 2021, summarizing optional expedients and exceptions for contracts, derivatives, and hedge accounting affected by the transition from interbank reference rates. Key provisions allow: treating certain contract amendments as modifications rather than extinguishments without significance testing; maintaining hedge accounting despite changes in critical terms through practical expedients; a one-time option to reclassify securities out of held-to-maturity; and, per the January 2021 update, treating changes to derivatives’ discounting, margining, or price-alignment rates as modifications. The guidance was effective upon issuance (March 12, 2020; January 7, 2021). The firm adopted selected expedients for contract modifications, hedge relationships, and discounting transition beginning in Q3 2020 (with the discounting transition election applied retrospectively) to ease administrative burden, with no material impact on its consolidated financial statements.

nodes.summary:

- Emphasizes that such statements are subject to significant risks and uncertainties beyond the Firm’s control, and actual results may differ materially.
- Outlines major categories of risk factors that could cause differences, including:
  - Macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions, including COVID-19 impacts, interest rate environment, and market liquidity/volatility.
  - Regulatory and legal changes and scrutiny (capital/liquidity, consumer practices, tax and trade/monetary/fiscal policy), and potential adverse proceedings.
  - Firm-specific operational and strategic risks: capital and liquidity management, credit quality of clients/counterparties, expense control, competition, product development/legacy liabilities, market acceptance/innovation, talent attraction/retention, control agenda and risk management/financial reporting controls, valuation challenges, and accounting standard changes.
  - Reputational, ESG, and sustainability considerations.
  - Operational resilience, including systems/security, third-party failures, and cybersecurity threats.
  - Disasters and extraordinary events (natural/man-made, pandemics, hostilities, climate-related effects).
  - Credit ratings changes and investor/consumer sentiment or behavior shifts.
- References additional risks in Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q and Part I, Item 1A of the 2020 Form 10-K.
- States that forward-looking statements speak only as of their date; the Firm does not undertake to update them, advising readers to consult subsequent filings for further disclosures.

- Consolidation policy: inclusion of JPMorgan Chase and entities where it has a controlling financial interest; elimination of intercompany items; client assets held in agency/fiduciary capacity excluded from the balance sheet; assessment of control via voting interest vs. variable interest entity models; references to 2020 Form 10-K Notes 1 and 14 for details.
- Offsetting policy: net presentation of derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral, and of securities financing activities, when legally enforceable master netting agreements and other specified conditions are met; the Firm has elected to net when conditions apply; reference to 2020 Form 10-K for further information.
- Direction to a Glossary of Terms and Acronyms (pages 163–171) for definitions used in the Notes.

nodes.title: Consolidation
nodes.heading: 1.1 Consolidation
nodes.start_phrase: The Consolidated Financial Statements include the accounts of JPMorgan Chase and other entities in which the Firm has a controlling financial interest.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase & Co. as a global financial services firm and reference to business segments (Note 25).
- Basis of presentation: unaudited interim Consolidated Financial Statements prepared under U.S. GAAP and applicable regulatory guidelines.
- Use of estimates and assumptions by management; inclusion of normal, recurring adjustments; interim statements should be read with the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Prior-period reclassifications to conform to current presentation, notably Q1 2021 reclassification of certain deferred investment tax credits from liabilities to other assets, increasing income tax expense and other income with no impact on net income; effective tax rate revised; no change to managed-basis results.
- Consolidation principles: inclusion of entities where the Firm has a controlling financial interest; elimination of intercompany items; fiduciary/agency assets excluded from the balance sheet.
