- Offsetting policy: net presentation of derivatives and related cash collateral, and certain securities financing activities, when legally enforceable master netting agreements and other specified conditions are met; further details referenced in the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Pointer to the Glossary of Terms and Acronyms for definitions used throughout the Notes.

nodes.title: Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.heading: 1.2 Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.start_phrase: U.S. GAAP permits entities to present derivative receivables and derivative payables with the same counterparty and the related cash collateral receivables and payables on a net basis on the Consolidated balance sheets when a legally enforceab le master netting agreement exists.
nodes.summary:
- Document section: Notes to JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s unaudited Consolidated Financial Statements; references a Glossary of Terms (pp. 163–171) and other notes in the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Firm overview: JPMorgan Chase is a Delaware-incorporated financial holding company with global operations across investment banking, consumer and small business banking, commercial banking, payments/transaction processing, and asset management; see Note 25 for segments.
- Basis of presentation: Financials prepared under U.S. GAAP and applicable regulatory guidelines; management uses estimates that affect reported amounts; interim results include normal recurring adjustments and should be read with the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Prior-period reclassifications: In Q1 2021, certain deferred investment tax credits were reclassified from accounts payable/other liabilities to other assets to reduce the carrying value of tax-oriented investments; this increased income tax expense and other income with no net income impact; prior periods (including effective tax rate) revised to conform; no change to managed-basis results.
- Consolidation policy: Includes JPMorgan Chase and entities where it has a controlling financial interest; all material intercompany items eliminated; client assets held in agency/fiduciary capacity are excluded from the balance sheet; control assessed via voting interest entity vs. variable interest entity frameworks (see 2020 Form 10-K Notes 1 and 14).
- Offsetting/netting: Derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral, and certain securities financing activities, are presented net when legally enforceable master netting agreements and other GAAP conditions are met; the Firm elects net presentation (see 2020 Form 10-K Note 1).
- Fair value measurement: Points to 2020 Form 10-K Note 2 for valuation methodologies, fair value hierarchy, and fair value treatment of assets, liabilities, and lending-related commitments.

nodes.title: Fair value measurement
nodes.heading: 2 Fair value measurement
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for a discussion of the Firm’s valuation methodologies for assets, liabilities and lending-related commitments measured at fair value and the fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and reference: Points to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for the Firm’s fair value methodologies, use of the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3), and valuation approach for assets, liabilities, and lending-related commitments measured at fair value.
- Comprehensive fair value tables: Presents detailed schedules of assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, disaggregated by:
  - Major product categories (e.g., federal funds and repurchase/resale agreements; securities borrowed; trading assets and liabilities by debt/equity instruments; derivatives by asset class; available-for-sale securities; loans at fair value; mortgage servicing rights; other assets; deposits; short-term borrowings; long-term debt; accounts payable and other liabilities; beneficial interests in consolidated VIEs).
  - Fair value hierarchy levels (Level 1, Level 2, Level 3).
  - Derivative netting adjustments under legally enforceable master netting agreements (reductions presented separately).
- Trading instruments detail:
  - Debt instruments broken out into U.S. GSE/government MBS (agency and nonagency residential and commercial), U.S. Treasury/GSE/government, municipals, CDs/commercial paper, non-U.S. government, corporate debt, loans, and asset-backed securities.
  - Equity securities, physical commodities, and “other” trading positions.
  - Derivative receivables and payables by asset class (interest rate, credit, foreign exchange, equity, commodity) with gross fair values by level and associated netting adjustments.
- Available-for-sale (AFS) securities: Category breakdowns for agency MBS (residential and commercial), U.S. Treasury/government, municipals, non-U.S. government, corporate debt, and ABS (including CLOs), shown by hierarchy level.
- Other fair value items: Loans measured at fair value (including residential and commercial first-lien mortgages and conforming loans intended for sale to GSEs), mortgage servicing rights at fair value, and other assets/liabilities measured at fair value.
- Key footnotes and clarifications:
  - U.S. GSE obligations included within certain government/MBS categories.
  - Physical commodities inventories accounted for at lower of cost or net realizable value, which approximates fair value; inclusion of all physical commodities inventories for consistent disclosure; discussion of hedge accounting reference.
  - Trading balances reflect reduction of long positions by identical short positions.
  - Certain investments measured at NAV as a practical expedient (e.g., hedge funds, private equity, real estate funds) are excluded from the hierarchy; amounts disclosed and split between trading and other assets.
  - Derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral are presented on a net basis when permitted; note that Level 3 balances would be lower if netting were applied.
  - Prior-period presentation revised to conform to current period.
- Level 3 valuations narrative:
  - Directs to the 2020 Form 10-K for the Firm’s valuation process and instrument-specific fair value techniques.
  - Describes that Level 3 instruments often include both observable (Level 1/2) and unobservable inputs; observable risks are risk-managed with Level 1/2 positions.
  - Explains disclosure of significant unobservable inputs, ranges, and weighted/arithmetic averages for primary Level 3 instruments, noting these statistics reflect instrument characteristics and portfolio mix rather than input uncertainty or estimate reasonableness.
  - Notes that ranges/averages will vary over time with changes in instrument underlyings, tenors, strikes, and portfolio composition.

nodes.title: Level 3 valuations
nodes.heading: 2.1 Level 3 valuations
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for further information on the Firm’s valuation process and a detailed discussion of the determination of fair value for individual financial instruments.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on fair value disclosures and hedge accounting context, with physical commodities inventories included for consistency across periods.
- Presentation notes:
  - Securities owned are shown net of identical securities sold short.
  - Certain investments measured at NAV practical expedient (e.g., hedge funds, private equity, real estate) are excluded from the fair value hierarchy; balances were $678m at March 31, 2021 ($55m trading; $623m other assets) and $670m at December 31, 2020 ($52m trading; $618m other assets).
  - Loans include residential first‑lien mortgages ($20.1b at March 31, 2021; $15.1b at December 31, 2020) and commercial first‑lien mortgages ($6.0b; $6.3b). Residential includes conforming mortgages intended for sale to U.S. GSEs ($11.9b; $8.4b).
  - Derivative receivables/payables and related cash collateral are netted when enforceable master netting agreements exist; Level 3 balances would be lower if netting (including cash collateral) were applied.
  - Prior periods revised to conform to current presentation.
- Level 3 valuation framework:
  - References the firm’s valuation process (2020 Form 10‑K, Note 2).
  - Level 3 instruments may include both observable and unobservable inputs; observable risks are hedged with Level 1/2 instruments.
  - Discloses ranges and weighted/arithmetic averages of significant unobservable inputs; these reflect instrument characteristics, not input uncertainty; values vary period to period.
- Level 3 instruments and key inputs as of March 31, 2021 (examples):
  - RMBS and loans ($991m): discounted cash flows; yield, prepayment speed, conditional default rate, loss severity.
  - CMBS and loans ($516m), corporate debt ($370m), loans ($1,579m), ABS ($54m): market comparables; price ranges and averages.
  - Net derivatives:
    - Interest rate ($130m): option pricing; IR volatility, spread volatility, IR and IR‑FX correlations; also DCF with prepayment speeds.
    - Credit ($(41)m): DCF; credit correlation, credit spreads, recovery, default and loss severity; also market comparable prices.
    - Foreign exchange ($(424)m): option pricing; IR‑FX correlation.
    - Equity ($(3,834)m): option pricing; forward equity price, equity volatility, equity and cross‑asset correlations.
    - Commodities ($(911)m): option pricing; forward commodity/power prices, volatility, correlation.
  - Mortgage servicing rights ($4,470m): discounted cash flows (details in Note 14).
  - Structured notes within long‑term debt, short‑term borrowings, and deposits ($27,985m): option pricing with unobservable inputs broadly consistent with derivative receivables; also DCF with credit correlation.
  - Other Level 3 assets/liabilities, net ($1,385m), including equity securities ($968m; $280m in Other Assets) valued using internal techniques (e.g., EBITDA multiples, comparable analysis); remaining items individually and in aggregate are insignificant.
- Footnote clarifications:
  - Product groupings may differ from balance sheet classifications; not all inputs apply to every instrument within a technique.
  - Price inputs assume par value of $100.
  - Forward equity price expressed as a percentage of current equity price.
  - Weighted averages used except for derivative inputs, where arithmetic averages are presented.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.heading: 2.2 Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 2 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K f or a discussion of the impact on fair value of changes in unobservable inputs and the relationships between unobservable inputs as well as a description of attributes of the underlying instruments and external market factors that affect the range of inputs used in the valuation of the Firm’s positions.
nodes.summary: Summary of JPMorgan Chase’s discussion on Level 3 fair value measurements and unobservable inputs. It references Note 2 of the 2020 Form 10-K for details on how changes in unobservable inputs and their interrelationships affect fair value, along with the attributes of underlying instruments and market factors that drive input ranges. The section presents rollforward tables of Level 3 financial instruments for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020. It clarifies that Level 3 classification is based on the significance of unobservable inputs, though these instruments also contain observable components. Reported gains and losses therefore reflect both unobservable and observable factors. It also notes that JPMorgan Chase risk-manages the observable components with Level 1 and Level 2 instruments, which are excluded from the tables, so the reported results do not capture the effects of those risk management activities.

nodes.title: Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.heading: 2.3 Changes in level 3 recurring fair value measurements
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables include a rollforward of the Consolidated balance sheets amounts (including changes in fair value) for financial instruments classified by the Firm within level 3 of the fair value hierarchy for the three months ended M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 and 2020 .
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: The excerpt discusses JPMorgan Chase’s Level 3 fair value measurements (instruments valued using significant unobservable inputs), including how changes in unobservable inputs affect valuations, and references Note 2 of the 2020 Form 10-K for methodology and input relationships.
- Level 3 rollforward tables: Detailed three-month rollforwards for March 31, 2021 and March 31, 2020 show beginning balances, total realized/unrealized gains or losses, purchases, sales, issuances, settlements, and transfers in/out of Level 3 for:
  - Assets: trading assets (debt and equity securities across MBS, municipals, non-U.S. government, corporates, loans, ABS), net derivative receivables (interest rate, credit, FX, equity, commodity), available-for-sale securities, loans, mortgage servicing rights (MSRs), and other assets.
  - Liabilities: deposits, short-term borrowings, trading liabilities, accounts payable and other liabilities, and long-term debt.
  - The tables also disclose changes in unrealized gains/losses related to instruments held at period-end and include footnotes on presentation (e.g., principal transactions revenue vs. mortgage fees).
- Interpretation nuances:
  - Level 3 classification is driven by the significance of unobservable inputs, though instruments may also include observable components; reported gains/losses therefore reflect both observable and unobservable factors.
  - Hedging/risk management positions in Levels 1 and 2 used to manage Level 3 exposures are excluded from the rollforwards.
  - All Level 3 derivatives are presented on a net basis irrespective of counterparty.
- Magnitude and mix:
  - Level 3 assets at fair value as a percentage of total Firm assets at fair value (including nonrecurring) were 1% at March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020; Level 3 liabilities as a percentage of total Firm liabilities at fair value were 8% and 9%, respectively.
  - Separately, Level 3 assets at fair value (including nonrecurring) were 0.5% of total Firm assets at March 31, 2021.
- Period movement highlights (Q1 2021):
  - Level 3 assets totaled $17.4 billion at March 31, 2021, up $952 million from year-end 2020, predominantly from a $1.2 billion increase in MSRs due to lower expected prepayment speeds amid higher rates.
  - No significant transfers between Level 2 and Level 3 during the quarter.
  - Reported total net gains: $984 million on assets (driven by MSRs) and $528 million on liabilities (largely long-term debt market movements).
- Prior-year stress period highlights (Q1 2020):
  - Significant transfers into Level 3 due to reduced market observability: about $2.1 billion of total debt and equity instruments (mainly trading loans) and gross transfers of $1.0 billion equity derivative receivables and $1.7 billion equity derivative payables.
  - Net gains: $1.2 billion on assets (gains in equity derivatives offset by MSR losses from faster prepayments on lower rates) and $4.6 billion on liabilities (long-term debt market movements).
- Credit and funding valuation adjustments (CVA/FVA) on derivatives (excluding hedges):
  - Q1 2021: CVA +$240 million; FVA +$105 million.
  - Q1 2020: CVA $(924) million; FVA $(1,021) million.
- Fair value option/DVA note:
  - Realized DVA on fair value option liabilities was not material in Q1 2021 and Q1 2020; unrealized DVA recognized in OCI was $(22) million in Q1 2021 and $(1.1) billion in Q1 2020.
- Administrative:
  - Transfers are recognized at the beginning of the quarter in which observability/significance changes occur.
  - Settlements include maturities, repayments, modifications, deconsolidations of VIEs, and other items.

nodes.title: Level 3 analysis
nodes.heading: 2.4 Level 3 analysis
nodes.start_phrase: Level 3 assets at fair value, including assets measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis, wer e 0.5% of total Firm assets at M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1.
nodes.summary:
- Reporting classifications:
  - Principal transactions revenue is the primary line for fair value changes, except CCB mortgage loans, lending-related commitments intended to sell, and mortgage loan purchase commitments, which are in mortgage fees and related income.
  - MSR fair value changes are reported in mortgage fees and related income.
  - Realized DVA on fair value option liabilities is in principal transactions revenue (not material for Q1 2021 and Q1 2020); unrealized DVA is in OCI ($(22) million in Q1 2021; $(1.1) billion in Q1 2020).
  - Loan originations are included in purchases.
  - Other changes include maturities, repayments, modifications, VIE-related deconsolidations, and similar items.

- Level 3 fair value analysis:
  - Level 3 assets at fair value (including nonrecurring) were 0.5% of total firm assets at March 31, 2021.
  - Level 3 assets measured on a recurring basis were $17.4 billion at March 31, 2021, up $952 million from December 31, 2020, driven mainly by a $1.2 billion increase in MSRs.
  - Transfers between levels:
    - Q1 2021: No significant transfers between Level 2 and Level 3.
    - Q1 2020: Significant transfers from Level 2 to Level 3 due to reduced observability/unobservable inputs—$2.1 billion in debt/equity instruments (mainly trading loans), $1.0 billion gross equity derivative receivables, and $1.7 billion gross equity derivative payables; no significant transfers from Level 3 to Level 2.
    - Transfers are based on changes in input observability/significance and assumed to occur at the period’s start.

- Gains and losses on recurring fair value instruments (excluding Level 1–2 risk management hedges):
  - Q1 2021: $984 million net gains on assets (MSRs benefited from slower prepayments amid higher rates); $528 million net gains on liabilities (market movements in long-term debt).
  - Q1 2020: $1.2 billion net gains on assets (equity derivative receivables gains offset by MSR losses on faster prepayments in lower rates); $4.6 billion net gains on liabilities (market movements in long-term debt).

- Credit and funding valuation adjustments (derivatives), impact on principal transactions revenue (excluding hedges):
  - Q1 2021: CVA $240 million; FVA $105 million.
  - Q1 2020: CVA $(924) million; FVA $(1,021) million.
  - FVA includes the firm’s own credit quality at inception and subsequent changes.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.heading: 2.5 Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis
nodes.start_phrase: The following tables present the assets and liabilities held as of March 31, 2021 and 2020 , for which nonrecurring fair value adjustments were recorded during the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020 , by major product category and fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary: The excerpt summarizes nonrecurring fair value measurements as of March 31, 2021 and 2020, by fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3) and product category, and shows related quarterly gains/losses. As of March 31, 2021, total assets measured on a nonrecurring basis were $2,542 million (Level 2: $1,869 million; Level 3: $673 million), comprising Loans of $2,160 million (Level 2: $1,857 million; Level 3: $303 million) and Other assets of $382 million (Level 2: $12 million; Level 3: $370 million). Liabilities were $14 million, all Level 3. As of March 31, 2020, total assets were $3,240 million (Level 2: $2,347 million; Level 3: $893 million), with Loans of $2,895 million (Level 2: $2,336 million; Level 3: $559 million) and Other assets of $345 million (Level 2: $11 million; Level 3: $334 million). Liabilities were $775 million, all Level 3. Other assets primarily include equity securities without readily determinable fair values measured under the “measurement alternative”; of the $370 million Level 3 assets in 2021, $316 million related to such equity securities, classified as Level 3 due to infrequent observable prices and/or share restrictions. Of the $303 million Level 3 loans in 2021, $137 million were residential real estate collateral-dependent loans valued using broker price opinions, appraisals, and automated valuation models with discounts of 13%–45% (weighted average 26%). Nonrecurring fair value changes for the three months ended March 31 were a net loss of $34 million in 2021 (Loans $(33) million; Other assets $2 million, including $6 million from the measurement alternative; Liabilities $(3) million) versus a net loss of $1,211 million in 2020 (Loans $(267) million; Other assets $(169) million, including $(154) million from the measurement alternative; Liabilities $(775) million). The note references additional details on collateral-dependent loans in Note 11.

nodes.title: Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.heading: 2.6 Equity securities without readily determinable fair values
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm measures certain equity securities without readily determinable fair values at cost less impairment (if any), plus or minus observable price changes from an identical or similar investment of the same issuer, with such changes recognized in other income.
nodes.summary:
- The firm applies the ASC 321 measurement alternative for equity securities without readily determinable fair values: carried at cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in identical or similar securities of the same issuer, with changes recognized in other income.
- When observable price changes occur, the firm may adjust prices to estimate fair value, considering differences in rights/obligations and aligning with its private equity valuation techniques.
- Select amounts (Other assets): carrying value was $2.3 billion at March 31, 2021 vs. $2.6 billion at March 31, 2020; quarterly upward carrying value changes were $7 million (2021) vs. $9 million (2020); quarterly downward changes/impairments were $(1) million (2021) vs. $(162) million (2020).
- The December 31, 2020 carrying value was $2.4 billion; period-end balances reflect cumulative purchases/sales and valuation adjustments. Securities with observable price changes are also reported in nonrecurring fair value disclosures.
- Cumulative adjustments from January 1, 2018 to March 31, 2021: upward $618 million; downward/impairment $(340) million.
- Included in other assets is an interest in approximately 40 million Visa Class B shares recorded at a nominal carrying value; these are restricted and will convert to Class A upon final resolution of related litigation. The Class B to Class A conversion rate was 1.6228 at March 31, 2021 and may be adjusted by Visa based on litigation developments.

nodes.title: Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value
nodes.heading: 2.7 Additional disclosures about the fair value of financial instruments that are not carried on the Consolidated balance sheets at fair value
nodes.start_phrase: The following table presents , by fair value hierarchy classification, the carrying values and estimated fair values at M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 , and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0, of financial assets and liabilities, excluding financial instruments that are carried at fair value on a recurring basis, and their classification within the fair value hierarchy.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Provides additional fair value disclosures for financial instruments not carried at fair value on the Consolidated balance sheets.
- Scope and timing: Compares carrying values to estimated fair values, classified within the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3), as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020; excludes instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis.
- Financial assets covered: cash and due from banks; deposits with banks; accrued interest and accounts receivable; federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements; securities borrowed; held-to-maturity investment securities; loans (net of allowance); and other assets. Assets are largely Level 1 for highly liquid balances, Level 2 for most receivables, securities financing, and portions of HTM securities, and Level 3 primarily for loans.
- Financial liabilities covered: deposits; federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements; short-term borrowings; accounts payable and other liabilities; beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs; and long-term debt. Most liabilities are Level 2, with some Level 3 components in other liabilities and long-term debt.
- Loans valuation methodology: Fair value generally estimated via discounted cash flow models incorporating loan terms (principal, rates, fees), expected lifetime credit losses, interest rates, prepayment assumptions, and market spreads; certain loans valued based on collateral. Differences between carrying and fair values reflect market interest rates, credit spreads, liquidity premiums, and other market factors, while carrying values reflect expected credit losses via the allowance.
- Off-balance sheet commitments: Presents carrying and estimated fair values (Level 3) for wholesale lending-related commitments; notes that amounts exclude the separately recognized guarantee liability and offsetting asset at inception and include the wholesale allowance for lending-related commitments. Consumer off-balance sheet lending-related commitments are not fair-valued because the firm can often reduce or cancel them.
- Reference: Points to JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K (page 173) for further details on valuing lending-related commitments.

nodes.title: Fair value option
nodes.heading: 3 Fair value option
nodes.start_phrase: The fair value option provides an option to elect fair value as an alternative measurement for selected financial assets, financial liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Explains the firm’s use of the fair value option (FVO) as an alternative measurement for selected financial assets, liabilities, unrecognized firm commitments, and written loan commitments. The FVO is used to reduce earnings volatility arising from mixed measurement bases and to align accounting with instruments managed on a fair value basis.

- Instruments elected for FVO:
  - Loans purchased/originated for securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation accounting, or otherwise managed on a fair value basis, including lending-related commitments
  - Certain securities financing agreements
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized financial assets containing embedded credit derivatives (that would otherwise require separate derivative accounting)
  - Structured notes (predominantly with embedded derivatives) issued in client-driven activities
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts where underlying assets are carried at fair value

- Presentation of results: Provides a table of changes in fair value recognized in the Consolidated statements of income for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020, split between principal transactions and all other income. The table includes only the elected instruments and excludes related risk management instruments that are required to be at fair value.

- Categories reported in the table:
  - Federal funds sold and securities purchased under resale agreements
  - Securities borrowed
  - Trading assets: debt and equity instruments (excluding loans)
  - Loans reported as trading assets: instrument-specific credit risk and other changes
  - Loans (non-trading): instrument-specific credit risk and other changes
  - Other assets
  - Deposits
  - Federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under repurchase agreements
  - Short-term borrowings
  - Trading liabilities
  - Other liabilities
  - Long-term debt

- Key period highlights (total changes in fair value recognized):
  - Long-term debt: gain of approximately $1.24 billion in 1Q21 vs. $4.19 billion in 1Q20; predominantly structured notes; related risk management impacts not included
  - Trading assets (debt/equity): gain of $621 million in 1Q21 vs. loss of $2.44 billion in 1Q20
  - Loans (instrument-specific credit risk): gain of $238 million in 1Q21 vs. $41 million in 1Q20
  - Loans (other changes): gain of $90 million in 1Q21 vs. $1.01 billion in 1Q20
  - Federal funds sold/resale and securities borrowed: losses in 1Q21 (−$12 million and −$70 million, respectively) vs. gains in 1Q20
  - Short-term borrowings: loss of $122 million in 1Q21 vs. gain of $1.72 billion in 1Q20

- Accounting notes and classifications:
  - For FVO liabilities, unrealized gains/losses due to instrument-specific credit risk (DVA) are recorded in OCI; realized DVA gains/losses are recorded in principal transactions (realized DVA was a $2 million loss in both 1Q21 and 1Q20)
  - Long-term debt at fair value is predominantly structured notes; table excludes the income statement impact of associated risk management instruments
  - Certain amounts are reported in mortgage fees and related income or other income, as indicated
  - Changes in fair value exclude contractual interest (recorded in interest income/expense except for certain CIB hybrid instruments); Note 6 provides further detail on interest recognition

nodes.title: Changes in fair value under the fair value option election
nodes.heading: 3.1 Changes in fair value under the fair value option election

  - Certain loans (e.g., securitization warehousing, subject to bifurcation, or managed on a fair value basis), including lending-related commitments
  - Certain securities financing agreements
  - Owned beneficial interests in securitized assets with embedded credit derivatives
  - Structured notes with embedded derivatives issued in client-driven activities
  - Certain long-term beneficial interests issued by CIB’s consolidated securitization trusts when underlying assets are at fair value
- Presents a table of changes in fair value recognized in the income statement for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020, by instrument category (e.g., federal funds and repos, securities borrowed, trading assets and loans, loans at fair value, deposits, repos/stock loaned, short-term borrowings, other assets/liabilities, and long-term debt).
- Clarifies that the table includes only instruments elected for FVO and excludes related risk management instruments that are required to be measured at fair value.
- Describes where fair value changes are reported: principal transactions revenue vs. other income, with certain items (e.g., mortgage-related items) reported in mortgage fees and related income, and some reported in other income.
- Notes treatment of instrument-specific credit risk:

- Highlights that long-term debt at fair value predominantly consists of structured notes; the table’s gains/losses do not include the P&L of risk management instruments used to hedge these notes.

nodes.title: Difference between aggregate fair value and aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding
nodes.heading: 3.2 Difference between aggregate fair value and aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding
nodes.start_phrase: The following table reflects the difference between the aggregate fair value and the aggregate remaining contractual principal balance outstanding as of M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, and D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0, for loans, long-term debt and long-term beneficial interests for which the fair value option has been elected.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Presents the difference between aggregate fair value and aggregate remaining contractual principal for items where the fair value option is elected, as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, covering loans, long-term debt, and long-term beneficial interests.
- Loans:

- Presentation: For fair value hedges, the Firm records gains/losses on hedging derivatives in the same income statement line as the related hedged items.
- 2021 Q1 results: Derivatives losses of $7,111 offset by hedged item gains of $7,481, yielding a net income statement benefit of $370 (interest rate $325; FX $18; commodity $27). Excluded components: -$78 (amortization) and $466 (current-period fair value changes). OCI impact from excluded components: -$37.
- 2020 Q1 results: Derivatives gains of $6,191 and hedged item losses of $5,758, netting $433 to the income statement (interest rate $299; FX $88; commodity $46). Excluded components: -$179 (amortization) and $351 (current-period fair value changes). OCI impact from excluded components: $115.
- Footnote highlights:
  - Interest rate hedges target benchmark rate risk (e.g., LIBOR) of fixed-rate long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded in net interest income; excludes inception hedge accounting adjustment amortization and interest accruals on swaps/hedged items.
  - FX hedges address spot foreign currency risk on long-term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges are overall fair value hedges of physical inventories (carried at lower of cost or net realizable value); impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
  - Excluded components (e.g., forward points, time value, cross-currency basis spreads) affect earnings via amortization over the derivative life or current-period fair value changes.
  - OCI reflects changes in the value of amounts excluded from effectiveness assessment under the amortization approach, predominantly cross-currency basis spreads, which are recognized in earnings over the derivative’s life.

- Focus: Impact of derivatives on the consolidated statements of income, with detailed disclosure of fair value hedge accounting results.

  - Breakdowns by contract type: interest rate, foreign exchange, and commodity derivatives, with gains/losses recognized in the same income statement lines as the hedged items.
- Accounting presentation and methodologies:
  - Interest rate hedges primarily of benchmark rate risk on fixed‑rate long‑term debt and AFS securities; gains/losses recorded in net interest income; certain inception adjustments and swap interest accruals excluded from the tables.
  - Foreign exchange hedges of spot FX risk on long‑term debt and AFS securities; impacts recorded primarily in principal transactions revenue and net interest income.
  - Commodity hedges of physical inventory (generally at lower of cost or NRV); impacts recorded in principal transactions revenue.
  - Excluded components (e.g., forward points, option time value, cross‑currency basis spreads) are recognized either via amortization over the derivative life or current‑period fair value changes; related OCI reflects changes in amounts excluded under the amortization approach.
- Balance sheet effects of fair value hedges:
  - Disclosure of cumulative fair value hedge basis adjustments embedded in carrying amounts of hedged items as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, split between active and discontinued hedging relationships.
  - Items covered: AFS investment securities, long‑term debt, and beneficial interests issued by consolidated VIEs.
  - These basis adjustments are expected to reverse through future net interest income as yield adjustments; positive amounts on assets reduce future NII, while positive (negative) amounts on liabilities increase (reduce) future NII.
- Key exclusions and clarifications:
  - Physical commodities inventories to which fair value hedge accounting is applied are carried at fair value; unrealized gains/losses recognized currently, with no incremental future net income impact upon exit.
  - Hedged items where only foreign currency risk is designated are excluded from the reversal analysis because related basis adjustments do not reverse through earnings; amounts excluded for AFS securities and long‑term debt are disclosed.

nodes.title: Securities financing activities
nodes.heading: 10 Securities financing activities
nodes.start_phrase: Refer to Note 11 of JPMorgan Chase’s 2020 Form 10-K for a discussion of accounting policies relating to securities financing activities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 10 summarizes JPMorgan Chase’s securities financing activities (repos, reverse repos, securities borrowing and lending), with cross-references to accounting policies (2020 Form 10-K Note 11), fair value option elections (Note 3), and assets pledged/collateral received (Note 23).
- Netting framework: Explains U.S. GAAP netting for securities financing agreements when supported by an appropriate legal opinion under a master netting agreement; related balances are netted on the Consolidated balance sheets. Collateral exchanged (cash or securities) reduces economic exposure but generally is not eligible for balance sheet netting and is shown as “Amounts not nettable” to reduce the “Net amounts.” Where no legal opinion is obtained, exposures are presented gross within “Net amounts.”
- Position summaries: Presents tables of gross, netted, balance-sheet-presented, and not-nettable amounts for:
  - Assets: securities purchased under resale agreements and securities borrowed.
  - Liabilities: securities sold under repurchase agreements and securities loaned/other.
  - Data is shown as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, highlighting that substantial gross balances are largely offset via netting and collateral, resulting in comparatively small net exposures.
- Fair value securities-for-securities lending: Notes significant securities-for-securities lending balances accounted for at fair value, where the firm as lender recognizes the securities received in other assets and the obligation to return them in accounts payable and other liabilities.
- Collateral and limits: Clarifies that amounts in the “not nettable” column are capped at the related net asset or liability with each counterparty; also identifies portions of activity where collateral rights exist but no qualifying legal opinion has been obtained.
- Collateral composition: Details the types of financial assets pledged in securities financing (e.g., U.S. Treasuries/GSE/government, non-U.S. government debt, MBS, corporate debt, ABS, equities) and presents gross liability balances for repos and securities loaned as of both dates.
- Maturity profile: Provides the remaining contractual maturity distribution (overnight/continuous, up to 30 days, 30–90 days, greater than 90 days) for repos and securities lending, showing concentration in overnight and short-term tenors.
- Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting: Discloses small amounts of transfers that failed sale accounting and are treated as collateralized financings; related assets are recorded in trading assets and loans, with corresponding liabilities in short-term borrowings.

Wholesale classes align with bank regulatory loan classifications; includes loans across CIB, CB, AWM, Corporate and certain risk-rated CCB loans. Reference to 2020 Form 10-K Note 14 for SPEs.

- Focus: Credit quality of retained residential real estate loans, with delinquency as the primary indicator.
- Coverage: Comparative tables as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020.
- Breakdowns provided:
  - Term loans by origination year (recent vintages through older cohorts; includes purchased loans by original vintage).
  - Revolving loans split between “within the revolving period” and “converted to term loans.”
- Metrics shown for each cohort:
  - Current, 30–149 days past due, 150+ days past due, total retained loans.
  - Percentage of loans 30+ days past due to total retained loans.
- Portfolio-level trends:
  - Total retained loans decreased from approximately $225.3B (12/31/20) to $219.2B (3/31/21).
  - 30–149 days past due declined (about $1.05B to $0.85B).
  - 150+ days past due declined slightly (about $1.19B to $1.15B).
  - Overall 30+ days past due rate improved from 0.98% to 0.90%.
- Vintage performance:
  - Very low delinquency in recent origination years.

nodes.title: Nature and extent of modifications
nodes.heading: Nature and extent of modifications
nodes.start_phrase: The Firm’s proprietary modification programs as well as government programs, including U.S. GSE programs, generally provide various concessions to financially troubled borrowers including, but not limited to,
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines the firm’s accounting and disclosure for residential real estate loan modifications, emphasizing that concessions to borrowers in financial difficulty are generally treated as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs). Short-term or otherwise insignificant changes that are not concessions, as well as modifications for which the firm elected to suspend TDR accounting under the CARES Act and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, are excluded. The carrying value of new TDRs was $251 million for the three months ended March 31, 2021, and $142 million for the same period in 2020. The firm had no additional lending commitments to borrowers with TDR-modified residential real estate loans.

Nature and extent of modifications: Through proprietary and government/GSE programs, concessions include interest rate reductions, term or payment extensions, and deferrals of principal and/or interest, with limited principal forgiveness. In Q1 2021 versus Q1 2020, 1,401 vs. 1,996 loans were approved for trial modifications and 1,714 vs. 1,481 were permanently modified. Among permanent modifications, 72% vs. 79% received interest rate reductions, 40% vs. 81% term/payment extensions, 31% vs. 11% principal and/or interest deferrals, 4% vs. 4% principal forgiveness, and 51% vs. 55% other actions (such as variable-to-fixed conversions and qualifying payment delays). Percentages exceed 100% because many loans receive multiple concessions. Reported figures exclude Chapter 7 discharge-only cases, short-term non-concession changes, and CARES Act/CAA TDR-suspended modifications.

Financial effects and redefaults: For loans with interest rate reductions, weighted-average rates declined from 4.57% to 2.91% in 2021 (5.20% to 3.48% in 2020). For loans with extensions, weighted-average remaining terms increased from 24 to 39 years in 2021 (22 to 39 years in 2020). No charge-offs were recognized upon permanent modification. Principal deferred totaled $12 million in 2021 ($5 million in 2020) and principal forgiven was $1 million ($2 million). Loans that redefaulted within one year of permanent modification had balances of $24 million in 2021 and $70 million in 2020. A payment default is defined as becoming two contractual payments past due; redefaults generally lead to foreclosure or similar liquidation, and near-term redefault rates may not reflect ultimate outcomes.

As of March 31, 2021, the weighted-average estimated remaining life of residential real estate loans permanently modified in TDRs was six years, incorporating expected voluntary and involuntary prepayments.

nodes.title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.heading: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of M a r c h 3 1 , 2 0 2 1 decreased when compared to D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 0, consisting of :
nodes.summary:
- Allowance for credit losses declined from December 31, 2020 to March 31, 2021, driven by:
  - $4.5 billion reduction in consumer, mainly in credit cards (improved macroeconomic scenarios) and residential real estate (better home price index expectations and some portfolio runoff).
  - $716 million net reduction in wholesale across lines of business due to improved macroeconomic scenarios.
- COVID-19 continued to distort key macroeconomic variables beyond model training ranges, increasing reliance on management judgment and model adjustments; these challenges have eased versus 2020 but persist.
- Despite economic improvement, uncertainties remain (labor market strength, vaccine efficacy against variants, potential lasting shifts in consumer behavior), prompting significant weighting on adverse scenarios.
- Adverse scenario assumptions: weighted average U.S. unemployment above 8% in 2021, about 6% into 2Q22; U.S. GDP returns to pre-pandemic level in 1Q22.
- Central case assumptions improved versus year-end:
  - At March 31, 2021: U.S. unemployment (quarterly averages) 2Q21 5.7%, 4Q21 4.8%, 2Q22 4.3%; cumulative real GDP change vs 12/31/2019 of 0.2%, 2.7%, 4.3%.
  - At December 31, 2020: unemployment 6.8%, 5.7%, 5.1%; GDP change −1.9%, 0.6%, 2.0%.
  - Future forecast changes will affect provision for credit losses.
- Note 13 – Variable interest entities (VIEs): overview of firm-sponsored VIEs and related accounting references.
  - By business segment:
    - CCB: credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts (servicing and securitization of originated and purchased residential mortgages).
    - CIB: mortgage and other securitization trusts (residential, commercial, other consumer loans); multi-seller conduits; municipal bond vehicles.
  - The firm also invests in and provides financing/services to third-party-sponsored VIEs.
- Significant firm-sponsored VIEs:
  - Credit card securitizations: JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary of the Chase Issuance Trust; see referenced tables for consolidated VIE assets and liabilities.
  - Mortgage and other securitization trusts: the firm securitizes originated/purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans, may act as servicer, and may retain beneficial interests.
- Cross-references to the 2020 Form 10-K (Notes 1 and 14) for consolidation policies, securitization involvement, and accounting treatment, and to specific Form 10-Q pages for detailed data.

nodes.title: Mortgage servicing rights
nodes.heading: Mortgage servicing right s
nodes.start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
nodes.summary:
- Defines mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as the fair value of expected future cash flows from servicing loans for others, valued based on estimated servicing fees and ancillary revenues minus servicing costs; MSRs are recognized when purchased or when loans are sold/securitized with servicing retained. MSRs amortize over time as servicing cash flows are received.
- Summarizes MSR activity for the three months ended March 31, 2021 vs. 2020:
  - Fair value rollforward (in millions): began at $3,276 (2021) vs $4,699 (2020); net additions of $584 vs $198 (originations and purchases net of dispositions); decrease from collection/realization of expected cash flows of $(187) vs $(248).
  - Valuation changes due to inputs/assumptions: +$797 (2021) vs $(1,382) (2020), driven primarily by changes in market interest rates and prepayment dynamics (+$836 vs $(1,370)); other model inputs/assumptions totaled $(39) vs $(12).
  - Ending fair value: $4,470 (2021) vs $3,267 (2020). Unrealized gains/(losses) included in income: +$797 vs $(1,382).
  - Operating metrics: contractual servicing and ancillary fees $291mm (2021) vs $364mm (2020); third-party mortgage loans serviced $444bn vs $506bn; servicer advances net $1.8bn vs $1.7bn, with minimal credit risk given seniority of reimbursement and rights to stop payments if collateral is insufficient.
  - Dispositions include transfers of excess MSRs into agency trusts in exchange for SMBS.
- Details mortgage fees and related income (CCB) for the quarter:
  - Production revenue increased to $757mm (2021) from $319mm (2020).
  - Net mortgage servicing revenue: operating revenue of $61mm (2021) vs $91mm (2020), reflecting loan servicing revenue offset by MSR amortization (cash flow realization).
  - Risk management results: MSR valuation gains from rates/other of +$836mm (2021) vs $(1,370)mm (2020) and other model changes of $(39)mm vs $(12)mm were more than offset by derivative and other hedging results of $(912)mm (2021) vs +$1,292mm (2020), yielding total risk management of $(115)mm (2021) vs $(90)mm (2020).
  - Total net mortgage servicing revenue was $(54)mm (2021) vs $1mm (2020); total CCB mortgage fees and related income were $703mm (2021) vs $320mm (2020); firmwide total mortgage fees and related income were $704mm (2021) vs $320mm (2020).
- Presents key MSR valuation assumptions and sensitivities:
  - Weighted-average constant prepayment rate (CPR): 10.28% at Mar 31, 2021 vs 14.90% at Dec 31, 2020; a 10% and 20% adverse change would reduce fair value by ~$195mm/$375mm (2021) vs ~$206mm/$392mm (2020).
  - Weighted-average option-adjusted spread (includes operational risk and regulatory capital): 6.65% (2021) vs 7.19% (2020); a 100bp and 200bp adverse change would reduce fair value by ~$197mm/$379mm (2021) vs ~$134mm/$258mm (2020).
  - Notes that sensitivities are hypothetical, not linear, and not necessarily additive due to interrelated assumptions.

nodes.title: Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.heading: Note 19 – Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.start_phrase: AOCI includes the after-tax change in unrealized gains and losses on investment securities, foreign currency translation adjustments (including the impact of related derivatives), fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges, cash flow hedging activities, net loss and prior service costs/(credit) related to the Firm’s defined benefit pension and OPEB plans, and fair value option-elected liabilities arising from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk (DVA).
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 19 explains Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI), detailing its components and period changes for the three months ended March 31, 2021 and 2020.
- AOCI components: after-tax unrealized gains/losses on investment securities; foreign currency translation adjustments (including hedges); fair value changes of excluded components on fair value hedges; cash flow hedge results; defined benefit pension and OPEB plan items; and DVA from changes in the Firm’s own credit risk on fair value option–elected liabilities.
- Q1 2021 movement: AOCI fell from $7.986 billion to $1.041 billion, an after-tax OCI loss of $6.945 billion.
  - Key drivers (after tax): unrealized losses on investment securities (−$4.339B) and cash flow hedges (−$2.249B); translation adjustments (−$250M); DVA (−$147M); fair value hedges (−$28M); partially offset by pension/OPEB (+$68M).
- Q1 2020 movement: AOCI rose from $1.569 billion to $7.418 billion, an after-tax OCI gain of $5.849 billion.
  - Key drivers (after tax): DVA (+$2.474B), cash flow hedges (+$2.465B), and unrealized gains on investment securities (+$1.119B); partially offset by translation adjustments (−$330M).
- Presentation: Tables show beginning balances, period net changes by component, and ending balances; and provide pre-tax, tax effect, and after-tax detail for each OCI component.
- Hedge-related details: Fair value hedge amounts reflect changes in cross-currency swap basis spreads excluded from effectiveness testing; related income recognition mechanics are noted.
- Reclassification adjustments: Where realized gains/losses are recorded in the income statement is specified (e.g., investment securities gains/losses; noninterest revenue, net interest income, and compensation for cash flow hedge reclasses).
- Transfers note: Unrealized gains included in AOCI related to AFS securities transferred to HTM totaled $2.9B at March 31, 2021 and $737M at March 31, 2020.

nodes.title: CECL regulatory capital transition delay
nodes.heading: CECL regulatory capital transition delay
nodes.start_phrase: As part of their response to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal banking agencies issued a final rule that provided the option beginning January 1, 2020 to delay the effects of CECL on regulatory capital for two years, followed by a three-year transition period beginning January 1, 2022 .

- Explains the federal banking agencies’ CECL regulatory capital transition rule allowing banks to delay CECL’s impact on regulatory capital for two years starting January 1, 2020, followed by a three‑year phase‑in beginning January 1, 2022.
- States JPMorgan Chase elected the CECL transition, excluding $4.5 billion from capital metrics as of March 31, 2021 (comprised of the $2.7 billion day‑1 retained earnings impact and 25% of the $7.0 billion increase in the allowance for credit losses since January 1, 2020, excluding PCD loans).
- Notes these CECL transition effects are reflected in Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, and total leverage exposure; references further details in Note 27 of the 2020 Form 10‑K.
- Presents Basel III Standardized and Advanced risk‑based and leverage‑based capital metrics for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. as of March 31, 2021 and December 31, 2020, indicating both entities were well‑capitalized and met all applicable requirements.
- Highlights key ratios and measures disclosed: CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital; risk‑weighted assets; CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital ratios; adjusted average assets; Tier 1 leverage ratio; total leverage exposure; and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR).
- Provides footnote clarifications: definition of adjusted average assets; temporary SLR relief that excluded on‑balance‑sheet U.S. Treasuries and Federal Reserve deposits for the holding company through March 31, 2021 (the bank did not elect this exclusion); confirmation that capital metrics reflect CECL transition provisions; and that PPP loans receive a 0% risk weight.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments
nodes.heading: Note 22 – Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase provides lending-related financial instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address the financing needs of its customers and clients.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 22 discloses JPMorgan Chase’s off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees, and other commitments, explaining their nature, risk, and accounting.
- Credit risk context: The contractual amounts represent the maximum possible credit exposure if commitments are drawn or guarantees called, but historically many are refinanced, extended, canceled, or expire without draw or default; thus totals are not indicative of expected future exposure or funding needs.
- Allowance and accounting: The Firm maintains an allowance for expected credit losses on wholesale and certain consumer lending-related commitments. Carrying values for lending-related products represent this allowance and any guarantee liability; for derivatives and items under the fair value option, carrying values are at fair value. References are made to Note 12 (allowance) and Note 28 of the 2020 Form 10-K (policies).
- Consumer line management: Total available credit for credit card, home equity, and certain scored business banking products is reported; the Firm can reduce or cancel such lines (often with notice as required) and typically closes credit card lines when borrowers are 60+ days past due. HELOCs may be reduced/closed due to property value declines or borrower credit deterioration.
- Reporting as of March 31, 2021 vs. December 31, 2020: A maturity breakdown (≤1 year, >1–3, >3–5, >5 years) is provided for contractual amounts and carrying values.
  - Consumer commitments: $730.6B total contractual (up from $715.8B), including $674.4B in credit card lines; residential real estate $44.7B; auto and other $11.6B. Carrying value for consumer commitments: $203M (primarily allowance/guarantee liability).
  - Wholesale commitments: $481.2B total contractual (up from $449.9B), including other unfunded commitments to extend credit $442.9B, standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees $34.8B, and other letters of credit $3.6B. Carrying value: $3.0B.
  - Total lending-related commitments: $1.212T contractual (up from $1.166T); total carrying value $3.214B (up from $2.753B).
- Other guarantees and commitments (contractual amounts unless noted):
  - Securities lending indemnification agreements and guarantees: $297.8B (collateral held $314.3B; primarily cash, G7 government, and U.S. GSE/agency securities).
  - Derivatives qualifying as guarantees: $53.6B contractual; $318M carrying value.
  - Unsettled resale and securities borrowed agreements: $154.2B; carrying value $3M.
  - Unsettled repurchase and securities loaned agreements: $108.4B; carrying value approximately zero.
  - Loan sale/securitization-related: Mortgage repurchase liability presented with carrying value only ($72M prior period); loans sold with recourse $823M contractual; $23M carrying value.
  - Exchange and clearing house guarantees/commitments: $84.9B (includes guarantees to the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation under the sponsored member repo program and other clearing memberships).
  - Other guarantees/commitments: $12.0B contractual; $59M carrying value (includes unfunded commitments to purchase secondary market loans, tax-oriented equity investments, and letters of credit hedged by derivatives).
- Presentation notes: Most consumer and wholesale commitments are U.S.-based. Certain wholesale amounts are shown net of risk participations in this note (disclosed amounts for netting), whereas regulatory filings present them gross. Prior-period amounts were revised for comparability.

It also summarizes derivatives that qualify as guarantees under U.S. GAAP: $53.6B of derivative guarantees notional, stable value contracts of $27.8B notional with maximum exposure capped at $2.8B, and $318M of derivative payables; the Firm also buys and sells credit protection via credit derivatives. Finally, it explains merchant charge-back risk in the Firm’s role as merchant acquirer, including the contingent liability when disputes favor cardholders and risk mitigation via withheld settlements, cash reserves, collateral, and a valuation allowance for expected charge-backs.

nodes.title: Litigation
nodes.heading: Note 24 – Litigation
nodes.start_phrase: As of March 31, 2021, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants, putative defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations and regulatory/government investigations.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Note 24 – Litigation, describing the Firm’s broad legal contingencies and select material matters. As of March 31, 2021, the Firm faces numerous private civil cases and regulatory/government investigations across business lines and geographies, ranging from individual suits to large class actions and involving diverse claims (tort, contract, antitrust, securities, consumer protection). The Firm estimates the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves at $0 to approximately $1.5 billion, noting that some matters cannot be estimated and that significant uncertainties (case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues like class certification, and unpredictable outcomes) mean actual losses may differ and estimates may change.

Material proceedings highlighted include:
- Amrapali (India): India’s Enforcement Directorate is investigating investments (2010, 2012) by offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan entities in Amrapali housing projects. The Supreme Court of India, overseeing homebuyer petitions since 2017, issued a July 2019 order with preliminary findings of violations of currency control and money laundering provisions, directing further inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, approximately $25 million held by JPMorgan India Private Limited was provisionally attached and subsequently transferred to a Supreme Court account; a separate FEMA civil proceeding is ongoing. The Firm is cooperating.
- Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation (UK): JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account (~$1.1 billion) for Nigeria’s government and two oil companies. After payouts in 2011 and 2013 per client instructions, the FRN sued in November 2017 in the English High Court for about $875 million, alleging the payments were part of a complex fraud not involving the bank but that the bank should have been on notice. Summary judgment was denied; trial is scheduled for February 2022.
- Foreign Exchange investigations/litigation: The Firm references prior settlements with government authorities regarding FX sales and trading activities and related controls, including a May 2015 plea; details continue beyond the excerpt.

- Interchange litigation: Merchants allege Visa/Mastercard and banks conspired to fix credit/debit interchange fees and enforce anticompetitive rules.
  - After an initial settlement (later reversed on appeal), the case split into monetary and injunctive tracks.

  - U.S. litigation: Mixed outcomes with dismissals and pending cases over BBA-era U.S. dollar LIBOR; SDNY certified antitrust classes relating to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants.

nodes.title: Interchange Litigation.
nodes.heading: Interchange Litigation.
nodes.start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
nodes.summary:
- Antitrust/FX matters: The Firm pled guilty to a single federal antitrust violation, was sentenced in January 2017, and completed probation in January 2020 in good standing. The U.S. Department of Labor granted a five-year ERISA QPAM exemption through January 2023; the Firm must reapply for the remainder of the ten-year disqualification period. A South Africa Competition Commission FX matter remains pending before the Competition Tribunal.
- FX civil litigation: SDNY approved in August 2018 a settlement of a consolidated U.S. class action alleging FX rate manipulation (including FX futures/options). Some class members opted out and sued in November 2018; several actions remain pending. Additional putative class actions were filed by consumers and indirect purchasers; in 2020 a $10 million settlement (with 11 other defendants) resolved the indirect purchaser case. Related individual and class actions have also been filed in the U.K., Israel, and Australia.
- Interchange litigation: Merchants allege Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks conspired to fix credit/debit card interchange fees and impose anticompetitive rules. A 2012 settlement was later reversed on appeal in 2017 and remanded. The case was split into monetary and injunctive classes. In September 2018, an amended monetary settlement added $900 million to about $5.3 billion in escrow; the District Court approved it in December 2019. Appeals are pending; due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive-relief case continues, and some individual merchant suits remain pending.
- LIBOR/EURIBOR investigations and litigation: JPMorgan Chase has responded to global inquiries concerning BBA LIBOR and EURIBOR. The Swiss competition probe into EURIBOR continues. In December 2016, the European Commission found an antitrust infringement related to EURIBOR; the Firm’s appeal to the EU General Court is pending. The Firm faces multiple LIBOR-related suits: some have been dismissed or resolved; others continue. SDNY certified an antitrust class concerning bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants. A consolidated class action concerning the ICE-era U.S. dollar LIBOR was dismissed; plaintiffs appealed. In August 2020, individual plaintiffs filed an antitrust suit alleging an unlawful agreement to set U.S. dollar LIBOR and attempted monopolization of LIBOR-based consumer lending/credit cards; in November 2020 they sought a preliminary injunction to halt LIBOR setting and enforcement of LIBOR-based instruments, which defendants opposed and which remains pending.

nodes.title: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.
nodes.heading: LIBOR and Other Benchmark Rate Investigations and Litigation.
nodes.start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase has responded to inquiries from various governmental agencies and entities around the world relating primarily to the British Bankers Association’s ("BBA") London Interbank Offered Rate (“LIBOR”) for various currencies and the European Banking Federation’s Euro Interbank Offered Rate (“EURIBOR”).
nodes.summary:
- Foreign exchange (FX) matters:

Similar actions have been filed outside the U.S. (U.K., Israel, Australia).

- Interchange fee litigation:
  - Merchants alleged Visa/Mastercard and banks conspired to fix credit/debit interchange fees and impose anticompetitive rules.

  - Related individual merchant actions against Visa/Mastercard and certain banks, including the Firm, remain pending.

- LIBOR and other benchmark rates:
  - Ongoing regulatory inquiries concerning LIBOR/EURIBOR, including a continuing Swiss COMCO EURIBOR investigation.
  - The European Commission issued a 2016 decision finding antitrust infringements related to EURIBOR; the Firm’s appeal to the General Court is pending.
  - Civil litigation includes multiple individual and class actions tied to U.S. dollar LIBOR and other benchmarks. Some actions were dismissed or resolved; others proceed.
  - SDNY certified antitrust classes for claims related to bonds and interest rate swaps sold directly by defendants.

  - Settlements of putative class actions concerning CHF LIBOR, SIBOR/SOR, and BBSW remain subject to court approval.

- Metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations and litigation:
  - Resolutions with DOJ, CFTC, and SEC addressed historic trading practices (2008–2016) in precious metals and U.S. Treasuries.
  - The Firm entered a DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement on two wire fraud counts; if obligations are met, charges will be dismissed after three years.

  - Putative class actions in SDNY allege precious metals futures/options manipulation under the CEA; consolidated and stayed through May 2021; similar putative class proceedings initiated in Canada.

- Securities lending antitrust litigation:

- Wendel (France):

Key highlights for 1Q21 vs 1Q20:

  - Lending (net interest income, fees, loan sale results, restructuring securities gains/losses, and credit portfolio risk management).
  - Fixed Income Markets (FX, rates, credit, commodities market-making).
  - Equity Markets (cash, derivatives, convertibles, prime brokerage).
  - Securities Services (custody, fund accounting/administration, securities lending, collateral management, depositary receipts).
  - Business metrics: Assets under custody (AUC) and Investment banking fees (advisory, equity/bond underwriting, loan syndication).

nodes.title: CORPORATE & INVESTMENT BANK (“CIB”)
nodes.heading: 11.2 CORPORATE & INVESTMENT BANK (“CIB”)
nodes.start_phrase:
Investment Banking: incorporates all revenue associated 
with investment banking activities, and is reported net of 
investment banking revenue shared with other LOBs.
nodes.summary:
- Defines key line-of-business metrics for Consumer & Community Banking (CCB) and Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB).
- CCB:
  - Debit and credit card sales volume: card purchase amounts net of returns.
  - Deposit margin/spread: net interest income as a percentage of average deposits.
  - Home Lending revenue split into:
    - Net mortgage servicing revenue: third‑party servicing income, MSR fair value changes, related risk management, gains/losses on excess servicing securitization, and gains/losses or lower of cost or fair value adjustments on certain government‑insured repurchased loans.
    - Production revenue: fees and income on loans originated for sale, including pipeline/warehouse risk management, gains/losses and lower of cost or fair value adjustments on held‑for‑sale loans (excluding certain government‑insured repurchases), and fair value option changes.
  - Mortgage origination channels: Retail (direct to consumer via bankers/branch/online/phone/referrals) and Correspondent (loans purchased from other institutions).
  - Credit Card business definition; net revenue rate as annualized net revenue over average loans.
  - Auto loan and lease origination volume: dollar amount originated.
- CIB:
  - Revenue definitions for Investment Banking (net of LOB sharing), Wholesale Payments (Treasury Services, Merchant Services, Trade Finance), Lending (NII, fees, loan sale and restructuring securities gains/losses, credit portfolio risk management), Fixed Income Markets, Equity Markets, and Securities Services (custody, fund admin, securities lending, collateral management, depositary receipts).
- Business metrics:
  - Assets under custody (AUC): safekeeping/servicing activities on which fees are earned.
  - Investment banking fees: advisory, equity underwriting, bond underwriting, and loan syndication.

nodes.title: COMMERCIAL BANKING (“CB”)
nodes.heading: 11.3 COMMERCIAL BANKING (“CB”)
nodes.start_phrase:
Commercial Banking provides comprehensive financial 
solutions, including lending, wholesale payments, investment 
banking and asset management products across three 
primary client segments: Middle Market Banking, Corporate 
Client Banking and Commercial Real Estate Banking.
nodes.summary:
- Commercial Banking (CB): Describes CB’s comprehensive financial solutions—lending, wholesale payments, investment banking, and asset management—delivered across three primary client segments: Middle Market Banking (small/midsized companies, local governments, nonprofits), Corporate Client Banking (large corporations), and Commercial Real Estate Banking (investors, developers, property owners across multifamily, office, retail, industrial, affordable housing). Notes an “Other” category for amounts not aligned with a primary segment.
- CB product revenue breakdown:
  - Lending: Secured financing (collateral such as receivables, inventory, equipment, real estate, other assets) including term loans, revolving credit, bridge financing, asset-based structures, leases, and standby letters of credit.
  - Wholesale payments: Products/services enabling clients to manage payments/receipts and invest/manage funds.
  - Investment banking: Capital-raising and risk/balance sheet solutions via advisory, equity underwriting, loan syndications; includes revenue from fixed income and equity market products used by CB clients.
  - Other: Primarily tax-equivalent adjustments from Community Development Banking and certain principal transactions income.
- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): Defines key terms and scope.
  - AUM: Assets managed on behalf of Private Banking, Global Institutional, and Global Funds clients; includes committed capital not called.
  - Client assets: AUM plus custody, brokerage, administration, and deposit accounts.
  - Multi-asset: Funds/accounts allocating AUM across multiple asset classes.
  - Alternative assets: Hedge funds, currency, real estate, private equity, and other nontraditional strategy funds.
- AWM lines of business:
  - Asset Management: Multi-asset investment solutions across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and money market funds for institutional and retail investors.
  - Global Private Bank: Services for high-net-worth clients including retirement, brokerage, custody, trusts/estates, loans, mortgages, deposits, and investment management.
- AWM client segments:
  - Private Banking: High- and ultra-high-net-worth individuals, families, money managers, business owners.
  - Global Institutional: Corporate/public institutions, endowments, foundations, nonprofits, governments worldwide.
  - Global Funds: Financial intermediaries and individual investors.
- Fund performance metrics (Asset Management):
  - Measures percentage of mutual fund AUM in funds rated 4- or 5-star.
  - Explains Morningstar ratings: risk-adjusted performance across time (overall rating weighted from 3-, 5-, 10-year where applicable); distribution by stars (5-star top 10%, 4-star next 22.5%, 3-star next 35%, 2-star next 22.5%, 1-star bottom 10%); U.S.-domiciled funds rated at share-class level.
  - Notes Nomura star rating based on three-year risk-adjusted performance only and that funds with under three years of history are not rated.

nodes.title: ASSET & WEALTH MANAGEMENT (“AWM”)
nodes.heading: 11.4 ASSET & WEALTH MANAGEMENT (“AWM”)
nodes.start_phrase:
Assets under management (“AUM”): represent assets 
managed by AWM on behalf of its Private Banking, Global 
Institutional and Global Funds clients.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Commercial Banking (CB): provides lending, wholesale payments, investment banking, and asset management to three core client segments—Middle Market Banking (small/midsize companies, local governments, nonprofits), Corporate Client Banking (large corporations), and Commercial Real Estate Banking (investors, developers, property owners). An “Other” category captures items not aligned to a segment.
- CB revenue by product:
  - Lending: secured financing (term loans, revolvers, bridge loans, asset-based structures), leases, standby letters of credit.
  - Wholesale payments: solutions for managing payments, receipts, liquidity, and funds.
  - Investment banking: capital-raising, advisory, equity underwriting, loan syndications, and market products used by CB clients.
  - Other: tax-equivalent adjustments from Community Development Banking and certain principal transactions income.
- Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) key definitions: AUM (includes committed but not called capital), client assets (AUM plus custody/brokerage/administration/deposits), multi-asset (allocations across multiple classes), and alternative assets (hedge funds, currency, real estate, private equity, other nontraditional strategies).
- AWM lines of business:
  - Asset Management: multi-asset solutions across equities, fixed income, alternatives, and money markets for institutional and retail clients.
  - Global Private Bank: wealth management for high-net-worth clients (retirement, brokerage, custody, trusts/estates, lending, mortgages, deposits, investment management).
- AWM client segments: Private Banking (HNW and UHNW individuals/families, money managers, business owners), Global Institutional (corporate/public institutions, endowments, foundations, nonprofits, governments), and Global Funds (financial intermediaries and individual investors).
- Asset Management performance metrics:
  - Percentage of mutual fund AUM in 4- or 5-star funds: based on Morningstar (overall rating from 3-, 5-, 10-year risk-adjusted performance; share-class level for U.S., primary share class elsewhere; Nomura 3-year rating in Japan). Excludes funds with <3-year history; values converted to USD; includes standard disclaimers that past performance is not indicative of future results.
  - Percentage of mutual fund AUM in 1st/2nd quartile (1-, 3-, 5-year): quartile rankings based on net-of-fee absolute returns; sourced from ranking providers; USD re-denomination; methodology varies by domicile (share class, primary share class, or fund level), with dual rankings where applicable; includes standard performance disclaimers.

structure.title: Risk Factors.
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
structure.start_phrase: The following discussion supplements the discussion of risk factors affecting the Firm as set forth in Part I, Item 1A: Risk Factors on pages 8-32 of JPMorgan Chase ’s 2020 Form 10-K .
structure.summary:
- Market Risk: Points readers to the Market Risk Management section of MD&A and pages 135–142 of the 2020 Form 10-K for quantitative and qualitative market risk disclosures.
- Controls and Procedures: CEO and CFO evaluated disclosure controls and procedures and concluded they were effective as of March 31, 2021; certifications provided in Exhibits 31.1 and 31.2. While committed to strong internal control over financial reporting, inherent limitations exist; no changes during the quarter that materially affected or are likely to materially affect internal control. Additional ICFR information referenced on page 158 of the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Legal Proceedings: Updates provided in Note 24 of this Form 10-Q, supplementing Part I, Item 3 of the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Risk Factors: Supplements 2020 Form 10-K risk factors (pages 8–32), emphasizing COVID-19 impacts, including market volatility, supply chain disruption, business closures, and unemployment. Negative effects on JPMorgan Chase include reduced demand and higher allowance for credit losses, with heightened model risk in estimating credit losses. Potential further impacts: increased credit losses, asset valuation declines, ratings downgrades, liquidity/capital constraints (e.g., elevated deposits, higher RWA, client rating downgrades, regulatory actions), and workforce disruptions. The severity and duration are uncertain and depend on pandemic trajectory, vaccine effectiveness, and government actions; stimulus and payment assistance may delay charge-offs. Participation in government support programs could increase scrutiny, litigation risk, costs, and reputational harm, and may amplify other existing risks.
- Supervision and Regulation: Directs readers to pages 3–7 of the 2020 Form 10-K.
- Unregistered Sales: No unregistered sales of equity securities during the quarter ended March 31, 2021.
- Share Repurchases: References Capital Risk Management in this 10-Q and the 2020 Form 10-K. Following the Federal Reserve’s December 18, 2020 guidance, the Firm resumed buybacks in Q1 2021; Board authorized up to $30 billion. Payouts (net repurchases plus common dividends) were capped at the average of net income over the prior four quarters, with restrictions extended through at least Q2 2021. In Q1 2021, the Firm repurchased 34,652,594 shares at an average price of $144.25, totaling $4.999 billion, leaving $25.001 billion under the authorization.
